questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
The matrix $Q$ is given below. Let ${q}_{1}$, ${q}_{2}$, and ${q}_{3}$ be the respective columns of $Q.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(Q).$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${q}_{3}={x}_{1}{q}_{1}+{x}_{2}{q}_{2}.$

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ -3 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $Q$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ -3 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 8 & 24\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{8}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$ is $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${q}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{3}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 3=6.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
The matrix $Q$ is given below. Let ${q}_{1}$, ${q}_{2}$,  ${q}_{3}$ and ${q}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $Q.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{q}_{1},{q}_{4}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(Q).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{4}$, where ${q}_{3}={x}_{1}{q}_{1}+{x}_{4}{q}_{4}.$ 

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 & -30 & -15 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 24 & 14\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $Q$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 & -30 & -15 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 24 & 14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=(-\frac{1}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 24 & 14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $4$th columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$ is $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2},{q}_{4}\}.$ 

So, we conclude that $B=\{{q}_{1},{q}_{4}\}$ is not a basis of $\text{Col}(Q).$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
The matrix $T$ is given below. Let ${t}_{1}$, ${t}_{2}$, and ${t}_{3}$ be the respective columns of $T.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{t}_{1},{t}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(T).$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${t}_{3}={x}_{1}{t}_{1}+{x}_{2}{t}_{2}.$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 3 & 8 & 30\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $T$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 3 & 8 & 30\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(T)$ is $\{{t}_{1},{t}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${t}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 30\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{t}_{3}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{t}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{t}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 3=6.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
The matrix $V$ is given below. Let ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{2}$,  ${v}_{3}$, and ${v}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $V.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(V).$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${v}_{4}={x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}.$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -3 & -3 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $V$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -3 & -3 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & -6 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 & 18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 & 18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(V)$ is $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $4$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${v}_{4}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ 12\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{4}}={{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=3\cdot 3=9.$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $Q$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ -3 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 8 & 24\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{8}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$ is $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${q}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{3}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{2}}.

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ -3 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $Q$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ -3 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 8 & 24\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{8}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$ is $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${q}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{3}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 3=6.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The matrix Q is given below. Let q1, q2, and q3 be the respective columns of Q. Determine if B={q1,q2} is a basis of Col(Q). If that is the case, find x1⋅x2, where q3=x1q1+x2q2.

Q=[128−320]

a
2
b
6
c
{q1,q2} is not a basis of Col(Q)
d
5
e
0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we reduce the matrix Q to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

Q=[128−320]R2:=R2+3R1∼[1280824]R2:=18R2∼[128013]R1:=R1+(−2)R2∼[102013]

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the 1st and 2nd columns. So, a basis of Col(Q) is {q1,q2}, that is to say,

B={[1−3],[22]}.

Now, since the 3rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express q3 as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

[80]⏟q3=(2)⏟x1⋅[1−3]⏟q1+(3)⏟x2⋅[22]⏟q2.

This gives us x1⋅x2=2⋅3=6.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $Q$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ -3 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 8 & 24\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{8}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$ is $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${q}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{3}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 3=6.$

Question 1

The matrix Q is given below. Let q1, q2, and q3 be the respective columns of Q. Determine if B={q1,q2} is a basis of Col(Q). If that is the case, find x1⋅x2, where q3=x1q1+x2q2.

Q=[128−320]

a
2
b
6
c
{q1,q2} is not a basis of Col(Q)
d
5
e
0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we reduce the matrix Q to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

Q=[128−320]R2:=R2+3R1∼[1280824]R2:=18R2∼[128013]R1:=R1+(−2)R2∼[102013]

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the 1st and 2nd columns. So, a basis of Col(Q) is {q1,q2}, that is to say,

B={[1−3],[22]}.

Now, since the 3rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express q3 as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

[80]⏟q3=(2)⏟x1⋅[1−3]⏟q1+(3)⏟x2⋅[22]⏟q2.

This gives us x1⋅x2=2⋅3=6.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
The matrix $Q$ is given below. Let ${q}_{1}$, ${q}_{2}$,  ${q}_{3}$ and ${q}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $Q.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{q}_{1},{q}_{4}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(Q).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{4}$, where ${q}_{3}={x}_{1}{q}_{1}+{x}_{4}{q}_{4}.$ 

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 & -30 & -15 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 24 & 14\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $Q$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 & -30 & -15 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 24 & 14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=(-\frac{1}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 24 & 14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $4$th columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$ is $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2},{q}_{4}\}.$ 

So, we conclude that $B=\{{q}_{1},{q}_{4}\}$ is not a basis of $\text{Col}(Q).$

Question 2
?

The matrix Q is given below. Let q1, q2, q3 and q4 be the respective columns of Q. Determine if B={q1,q4} is a basis of Col(Q). If that is the case, find x1⋅x4, where q3=x1q1+x4q4.

Q=[−50−30−150363402414]

a
12
b
9
c
{q1,q4} is not a basis of Col(Q)
d
−8
e
−6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we reduce the matrix Q to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

Q=[−50−30−150363402414]R1:=(−15)R1∼[10630363402414]R3:=R3+(−4)R1∼[106303630002]R2:=13R2∼[106301210002]R3:=12R3∼[106301210001]

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the 1st, 2nd, and 4th columns. So, a basis of Col(Q) is {q1,q2,q4}.

So, we conclude that B={q1,q4} is not a basis of Col(Q).

solution.reasoning: B does not span Col(Q). If q₃=x₁q₁+x₄q₄, the second row forces x₄=2, and the first row then forces x₁=0. But the third row would give 24=28, a contradiction. Thus B is not a basis. No captured Math Academy answer evidence is provided.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
The matrix $Q$ is given below. Let ${q}_{1}$, ${q}_{2}$,  ${q}_{3}$ and ${q}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $Q.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{q}_{1},{q}_{4}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(Q).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{4}$, where ${q}_{3}={x}_{1}{q}_{1}+{x}_{4}{q}_{4}.$ 

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 & -30 & -15 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 24 & 14\end{aligned}]
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $Q$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 & -30 & -15 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 24 & 14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=(-\frac{1}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 24 & 14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $4$th columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$ is $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2},{q}_{4}\}.$ 

So, we conclude that $B=\{{q}_{1},{q}_{4}\}$ is not a basis of $\text{Col}(Q).$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
The matrix $T$ is given below. Let ${t}_{1}$, ${t}_{2}$, and ${t}_{3}$ be the respective columns of $T.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{t}_{1},{t}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(T).$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${t}_{3}={x}_{1}{t}_{1}+{x}_{2}{t}_{2}.$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 3 & 8 & 30\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $T$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 3 & 8 & 30\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(T)$ is $\{{t}_{1},{t}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${t}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 30\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{t}_{3}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{t}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{t}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 3=6.$

The matrix T is given below. Let t1, t2, and t3 be the respective columns of T. Determine if B={t1,t2} is a basis of Col(T). If that is the case, find x1⋅x2, where t3=x1t1+x2t2.

T=[1283830]

a
3
b
6
c
5
d
−3
e
{t1,t2} is not a basis of Col(T)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we reduce the matrix T to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

T=[1283830]R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[128026]R2:=12R2∼[128013]R1:=R1+(−2)R2∼[102013]

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the 1st and 2nd columns. So, a basis of Col(T) is {t1,t2}, that is to say,

B={[13],[28]}.

Now, since the 3rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express t3 as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

[830]⏟t3=(2)⏟x1⋅[13]⏟t1+(3)⏟x2⋅[28]⏟t2.

This gives us x1⋅x2=2⋅3=6.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $T$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 3 & 8 & 30\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(T)$ is $\{{t}_{1},{t}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${t}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 30\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{t}_{3}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{t}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{t}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 3=6.$

{t1,t2} is not a basis of Col(T)

Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we reduce the matrix T to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

T=[1283830]R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[128026]R2:=12R2∼[128013]R1:=R1+(−2)R2∼[102013]

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the 1st and 2nd columns. So, a basis of Col(T) is {t1,t2}, that is to say,

B={[13],[28]}.

Now, since the 3rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express t3 as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

[830]⏟t3=(2)⏟x1⋅[13]⏟t1+(3)⏟x2⋅[28]⏟t2.

This gives us x1⋅x2=2⋅3=6.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
The matrix $V$ is given below. Let ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{2}$,  ${v}_{3}$, and ${v}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $V.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(V).$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${v}_{4}={x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}.$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -3 & -3 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $V$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -3 & -3 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & -6 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 & 18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 & 18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(V)$ is $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $4$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${v}_{4}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ 12\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{4}}={{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=3\cdot 3=9.$

V=[10−131−2−3−3−26812]

a
−6
b
9
c
{v1,v2} is not a basis of Col(V)
d
5
e
4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we reduce the matrix V to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

V=[10−131−2−3−3−26812]R2:=R2+(−1)R1∼[10−130−2−2−6−26812]R3:=R3+2R1∼[10−130−2−2−606618]R2:=(−12)R2∼[10−13011306618]R3:=R3+(−6)R2∼[10−1301130000]

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the 1st and 2nd columns. So, a basis of Col(V) is {v1,v2}, that is to say, B={[11−2],[0−26]}.

Now, since the 4th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express v4 as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

[3−312]⏟v4=(3)⏟x1⋅[11−2]⏟v1+(3)⏟x2⋅[0−26]⏟v2.

This gives us x1⋅x2=3⋅3=9.

question.html:
Question 5
?

The matrix V is given below. Let v1, v2, v3, and v4 be the respective columns of V. Determine if B={v1,v2} is a basis of Col(V). If that is the case, find x1⋅x2, where v4=x1v1+x2v2.

V=[10−131−2−3−3−26812]

a
−6
b
9
c
{v1,v2} is not a basis of Col(V)
d
5
e
4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we reduce the matrix V to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

V=[10−131−2−3−3−26812]R2:=R2+(−1)R1∼[10−130−2−2−6−26812]R3:=R3+2R1∼[10−130−2−2−606618]R2:=(−12)R2∼[10−13011306618]R3:=R3+(−6)R2∼[10−1301130000]

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the 1st and 2nd columns. So, a basis of Col(V) is {v1,v2}, that is to say, B={[11−2],[0−26]}.

Now, since the 4th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express v4 as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

[3−312]⏟v4=(3)⏟x1⋅[11−2]⏟v1+(3)⏟x2⋅[0−26]⏟v2.

This gives us x1⋅x2=3⋅3=9.

solution.reasoning: The columns v₁ and v₂ are independent: av₁+bv₂=0 forces a=0 from the first coordinate and b=0 from the second. Also v₃=−v₁+v₂ and v₄=3v₁+3v₂, so B spans Col(V) and is a basis. Thus x₁x₂=3·3=9. No captured Math Academy answer evidence is provided.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
The matrix $V$ is given below. Let ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{2}$,  ${v}_{3}$, and ${v}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $V.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(V).$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${v}_{4}={x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}.$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -3 & -3 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}]
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $V$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -3 & -3 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & -6 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 & 18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 & 18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(V)$ is $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $4$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${v}_{4}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ 12\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{4}}={{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=3\cdot 3=9.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity $2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y).$
questions.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\,2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+y) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+y)-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$
questions.worked_solution:
$$

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Notice that we do not have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
{cosh}^{2}⁡x\,-\,{sinh}^{2}⁡x=1.
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity $\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$
questions.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,-\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y.
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$
questions.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

Notice that we do not have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡y+\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y.
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
$$

Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x{sech}^{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity 

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

$$
\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral using the above identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x{sech}^{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\cdot {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x})}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-\operatorname{tanh}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}-0 \\  & =\frac{2-{2}^{-1}}{2+{2}^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2-\frac{1}{2}}{2+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{3}{2}}{\frac{5}{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
$$

Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{coth}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{sech}⁡x\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identities corresponding to the trigonometric identities 

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{ and }\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identities are

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\,\text{ and }\,\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral using the above identities, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{coth}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{sech}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sinh}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cosh}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-\operatorname{sinh}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{0}-{e}^{-0}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2-{2}^{-1}}{2}-\frac{1-1}{2} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1/2)}^{0}\frac{\operatorname{tanh}⁡x}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

$$

First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1/2)}^{0}\frac{\operatorname{tanh}⁡x}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1/2)}^{0}\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now we find the hyperbolic identities corresponding to the trigonometric identities 

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{ and }\,\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identities are

$$
\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}\,\text{ and }\,\operatorname{tanh}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}.
$$

Then, we use the above identities to write the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1/2)}^{0}\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1/2)}^{0}\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\cdot {sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{sech}^{2}⁡x{|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1/2)}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{sech}^{2}⁡(0)+\frac{1}{2}{sech}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡1/2) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{4}{({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡1/2}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡1/2})^{2}}-\frac{4}{({e}^{0}+{e}^{0})^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{2}{(1/2+2)^{2}}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{9}{50}\end{aligned}

questions.problem: ${\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
$$

$$

First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\text{d}x.

Now, we need to find the hyperbolic identities that correspond to the following trigonometric identities: 

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identities are

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x},\,\,\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Then, we use the above identities to express the integral as

$$
{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{csch}⁡x{|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\  & =-\operatorname{csch}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)+\operatorname{csch}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =-\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}+\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{4-{4}^{-1}}+\frac{2}{2-{2}^{-1}} \\  & =-\frac{8}{15}+\frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
$$

$$

$$
\int \frac{5\operatorname{coth}⁡x-3\operatorname{csch}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}(5\operatorname{coth}⁡x-3\operatorname{csch}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

Now, recall the following identity:

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}
$$

Then, we use the above identity to express the integral as

$$
\int \operatorname{csch}⁡x(5\operatorname{coth}⁡x-3\operatorname{csch}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5\operatorname{coth}⁡x-3\operatorname{csch}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{csch}⁡x(5\operatorname{coth}⁡x-3\operatorname{csch}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \operatorname{coth}⁡x\operatorname{csch}⁡x\,\text{d}x-3\int {csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-5\operatorname{csch}⁡x+3\operatorname{coth}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
$$

Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{{coth}^{2}⁡x}{2{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

$$

First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{{coth}^{2}⁡x}{2{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {coth}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now we need to find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity 

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Then, we use the above identity to write the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {coth}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{csch}^{2}⁡x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡x{|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)-\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+1}{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-1}-\frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+1}{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{5}{3}-\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =\frac{5}{24}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {tanh}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{sech}^{2}⁡x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tanh}⁡x{|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-1}{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+1}-\frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-1}{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{4}{5}-\frac{3}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem:
$$

Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{coth}⁡x}{{csch}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identities that correspond to the following trigonometric identities:

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identities are

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{coth}⁡x}{{csch}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\operatorname{coth}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{csch}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\cdot {sinh}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\frac{5}{3}$ |

Now, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{5/3}u\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}{|}_{1}^{5/3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({(\frac{5}{3})}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{25}{9}-1) \\  & =\frac{8}{9}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem:
$$

Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}2\operatorname{csch}⁡(2x)\operatorname{coth}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identities that correspond to the following trigonometric identities:

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identities are

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}2\operatorname{csch}⁡(2x)\operatorname{coth}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\operatorname{csch}⁡(2x)\operatorname{coth}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2x)}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2x.$

| $x$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡16$ |

Now, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\operatorname{csch}⁡(2x)\operatorname{coth}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡16}\operatorname{csch}⁡(u)\operatorname{coth}⁡(u)\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{csch}⁡(u){|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡16} \\  & =-\operatorname{csch}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡16)+\operatorname{csch}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡16)}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(\frac{16-{16}^{-1}}{2})}+\frac{1}{(\frac{4-{4}^{-1}}{2})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(\frac{255}{32})}+\frac{1}{(\frac{15}{8})} \\  & =\frac{104}{255}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 18
questions.problem:
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{3}}\operatorname{coth}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the following trigonometric identity:

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{3}}\operatorname{coth}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{3}}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x.$

| $x$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{3}{4}$ | $\frac{4}{3}$ |

Now, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{3}}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{3/4}^{4/3}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3/4}^{4/3}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{3/4}^{4/3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\int {sech}^{4}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
$$

First, recall the following identity:

$$
\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}
$$

Then, we use the above identity and rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {sech}^{4}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{cosh}^{4}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{cosh}^{4}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{4}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3{cosh}^{3}⁡x}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{sech}^{3}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$

${\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\operatorname{coth}⁡x{csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identities that correspond to the following trigonometric identities:

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identities are

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\operatorname{coth}⁡x{csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\cdot {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x})}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{{sinh}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x.$

| $x$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{3}{4}$ | $\frac{4}{3}$ |

Now, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{{sinh}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{3/4}^{4/3}\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{3/4}^{4/3}{u}^{-3}\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{-3+1}}{-3+1}\,{|}_{3/4}^{4/3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}}\,{|}_{3/4}^{4/3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{(\frac{4}{3})}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{9}{32}+\frac{8}{9} \\  & =\frac{175}{288}\end{aligned}
$$

Introduction
?

It's possible to convert every trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity using Osborn's rule.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, change the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

To demonstrate, consider the Pythagorean trigonometric identity:

Notice that this trigonometric identity contains a product of two sines. Therefore, to find the corresponding hyperbolic identity, we change each trigonometric function to its corresponding hyperbolic counterpart and change the sign in front of the corresponding product of sines.

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity 2sin⁡xsin⁡y=cos⁡(x−y)−cos⁡(x+y).

a
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=sinh⁡(x−y)+sinh⁡(x+y)
b
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)−cosh⁡(x+y)
c
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)+cosh⁡(x+y)
d
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x+y)−cosh⁡(x−y)
e
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=sinh⁡(x+y)−sinh⁡(x−y)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity: 2sin⁡xsin⁡y=cos⁡(x−y)−cos⁡(x+y)

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is −2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)−cosh⁡(x+y)2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x+y)−cosh⁡(x−y).

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x.

a
sinh⁡2x=sinh2⁡x−cosh2⁡x
b
sinh⁡2x=−2sinh⁡xcosh⁡x
c

d

e

Submit
Incorrect

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x

sinh⁡2x=2sinh⁡xcosh⁡x.

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity cos2⁡x+sin2⁡x=1.

a
cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=1
b
cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=−1
c
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=1
d
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=−1
e
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=e
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

cos2⁡x+sin2⁡x=1

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=1.

\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity cos⁡(x−y)=cos⁡xcos⁡y+sin⁡xsin⁡y.

a
cosh⁡(x−y)=cosh⁡xcosh⁡y+sinh⁡xsinh⁡y
b
cosh⁡(x−y)=sinh⁡xsinh⁡y−cosh⁡xcosh⁡y
c
cosh⁡(x−y)=2cosh⁡xcosh⁡y
d
cosh⁡(x−y)=−2cosh⁡xcosh⁡y
e
cosh⁡(x−y)=cosh⁡xcosh⁡y−sinh⁡xsinh⁡y
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity: cos⁡(x−y)=cos⁡xcos⁡y+sin⁡xsin⁡y

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is cosh⁡(x−y)=cosh⁡xcosh⁡y−sinh⁡xsinh⁡y.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Deriving a Hyperbolic Identity Using Osborn's Rule
observed_steps.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

Notice that we do not have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡y+\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity sin⁡(x+y)=sin⁡xcos⁡y+cos⁡xsin⁡y.

a
sinh⁡(x+y)=sinh⁡xcosh⁡y+cosh⁡xsinh⁡y
b
sinh⁡(x+y)=cosh⁡xsinh⁡y−sinh⁡xcosh⁡y
c
sinh⁡(x+y)=cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡y
d
sinh⁡(x+y)=sinh⁡xcosh⁡y−cosh⁡xsinh⁡y
e
sinh⁡(x+y)=sinh2⁡x+sinh2⁡y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity: sin⁡(x+y)=sin⁡xcos⁡y+cos⁡xsin⁡y

Notice that we do not have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is sinh⁡(x+y)=sinh⁡xcosh⁡y+cosh⁡xsinh⁡y.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity 

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

$$
\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral using the above identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x{sech}^{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\cdot {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x})}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-\operatorname{tanh}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}-0 \\  & =\frac{2-{2}^{-1}}{2+{2}^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2-\frac{1}{2}}{2+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{3}{2}}{\frac{5}{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the following trigonometric identity:

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{3}}\operatorname{coth}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{3}}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x.$

| $x$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{3}{4}$ | $\frac{4}{3}$ |

Now, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{3}}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{3/4}^{4/3}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3/4}^{4/3}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{3/4}^{4/3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, recall the following identity: sech⁡x=1cosh⁡x

Then, we use the above identity and rewrite the integral as follows: ∫sech4⁡xsinh⁡xdx=∫1cosh4⁡x⋅sinh⁡xdx

We can solve this by substitution. Let u=cosh⁡x. Then dudx=sinh⁡x⟹du=sinh⁡xdx.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and compute it, as follows:

∫1cosh4⁡x⋅sinh⁡xdx=∫1u4du=−13u3+C=−13cosh3⁡x+C=−13sech3⁡x+C

First, we find the hyperbolic identities that correspond to the following trigonometric identities:

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identities are

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\operatorname{coth}⁡x{csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\cdot {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x})}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{{sinh}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x.$

| $x$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{3}{4}$ | $\frac{4}{3}$ |

Now, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{{sinh}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{3/4}^{4/3}\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{3/4}^{4/3}{u}^{-3}\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{-3+1}}{-3+1}\,{|}_{3/4}^{4/3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}}\,{|}_{3/4}^{4/3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{(\frac{4}{3})}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{9}{32}+\frac{8}{9} \\  & =\frac{175}{288}\end{aligned}
$$

steps.title: Introduction
steps.html:
Introduction
?

It's possible to convert every trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity using Osborn's rule.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, change the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

To demonstrate, consider the Pythagorean trigonometric identity:

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity $2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y).$
question.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\,2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+y) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+y)-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity 2sin⁡xsin⁡y=cos⁡(x−y)−cos⁡(x+y).

a
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=sinh⁡(x−y)+sinh⁡(x+y)
b
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)−cosh⁡(x+y)
c
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)+cosh⁡(x+y)
d
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x+y)−cosh⁡(x−y)
e
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=sinh⁡(x+y)−sinh⁡(x−y)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity: 2sin⁡xsin⁡y=cos⁡(x−y)−cos⁡(x+y)

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is −2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)−cosh⁡(x+y)2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x+y)−cosh⁡(x−y).

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Deriving a Hyperbolic Identity Using Osborn's Rule
last_observation.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\,2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+y) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+y)-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity 2sin⁡xsin⁡y=cos⁡(x−y)−cos⁡(x+y).

a
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=sinh⁡(x−y)+sinh⁡(x+y)
b
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)−cosh⁡(x+y)
c
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)+cosh⁡(x+y)
d
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x+y)−cosh⁡(x−y)
e
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=sinh⁡(x+y)−sinh⁡(x−y)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity: 2sin⁡xsin⁡y=cos⁡(x−y)−cos⁡(x+y)

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is −2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)−cosh⁡(x+y)2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x+y)−cosh⁡(x−y).
question.knowledge_point: Deriving a Hyperbolic Identity Using Osborn's Rule

solution.reasoning: The addition formulas give cosh(x+y)=cosh(x)cosh(y)+sinh(x)sinh(y) and cosh(x-y)=cosh(x)cosh(y)-sinh(x)sinh(y). Subtraction yields option d. The mathematics is certain, but no Math Academy answer or grade for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity $2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y).$
feedback.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\,2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+y) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+y)-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity 2sin⁡xsin⁡y=cos⁡(x−y)−cos⁡(x+y).

a
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=sinh⁡(x−y)+sinh⁡(x+y)
b
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)−cosh⁡(x+y)
c
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)+cosh⁡(x+y)
d
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x+y)−cosh⁡(x−y)
e
2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=sinh⁡(x+y)−sinh⁡(x−y)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity: 2sin⁡xsin⁡y=cos⁡(x−y)−cos⁡(x+y)

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is −2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x−y)−cosh⁡(x+y)2sinh⁡xsinh⁡y=cosh⁡(x+y)−cosh⁡(x−y).

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$
question.worked_solution:
$$

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Notice that we do not have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x.
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x.

a
sinh⁡2x=sinh2⁡x−cosh2⁡x
b
sinh⁡2x=−2sinh⁡xcosh⁡x
c
sinh⁡2x=12sinh⁡xcosh⁡x
d
sinh⁡2x=sinh2⁡x+cosh2⁡x
e
sinh⁡2x=2sinh⁡xcosh⁡x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x

Notice that we do not have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

sinh⁡2x=2sinh⁡xcosh⁡x.
question.knowledge_point: Deriving a Hyperbolic Identity Using Osborn's Rule

solution.reasoning: The hyperbolic addition formula gives sinh(2x)=sinh(x)cosh(x)+cosh(x)sinh(x)=2sinh(x)cosh(x), so option e is correct. No sign change is needed because there is no product of two sines. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$
feedback.worked_solution:
$$

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Notice that we do not have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x.
$$

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x.

a
sinh⁡2x=sinh2⁡x−cosh2⁡x
b
sinh⁡2x=−2sinh⁡xcosh⁡x
c
sinh⁡2x=12sinh⁡xcosh⁡x
d
sinh⁡2x=sinh2⁡x+cosh2⁡x
e
sinh⁡2x=2sinh⁡xcosh⁡x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x

Notice that we do not have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

sinh⁡2x=2sinh⁡xcosh⁡x.

question.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1.$
question.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
{cosh}^{2}⁡x\,-\,{sinh}^{2}⁡x=1.
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity cos2⁡x+sin2⁡x=1.

a
cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=1
b
cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=−1
c
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=1
d
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=−1
e
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=e
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

cos2⁡x+sin2⁡x=1

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=1.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Deriving a Hyperbolic Identity Using Osborn's Rule
last_observation.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
{cosh}^{2}⁡x\,-\,{sinh}^{2}⁡x=1.
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity cos2⁡x+sin2⁡x=1.

a
cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=1
b
cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=−1
c
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=1
d
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=−1
e
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=e
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

cos2⁡x+sin2⁡x=1

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=1.
question.knowledge_point: Deriving a Hyperbolic Identity Using Osborn's Rule

solution.reasoning: Replacing the functions by their hyperbolic counterparts and reversing the sign of the squared sine term gives cosh²(x)−sinh²(x)=1, option a. This also follows directly from the exponential definitions. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question was captured.

feedback.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1.$
feedback.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
{cosh}^{2}⁡x\,-\,{sinh}^{2}⁡x=1.
$$

feedback.html:
Question 3
?

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity cos2⁡x+sin2⁡x=1.

a
cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=1
b
cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=−1
c
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=1
d
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=−1
e
cosh2⁡x+sinh2⁡x=e
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

cos2⁡x+sin2⁡x=1

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

cosh2⁡x−sinh2⁡x=1.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity $\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$
question.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,-\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y.
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity cos⁡(x−y)=cos⁡xcos⁡y+sin⁡xsin⁡y.

a
cosh⁡(x−y)=cosh⁡xcosh⁡y+sinh⁡xsinh⁡y
b
cosh⁡(x−y)=sinh⁡xsinh⁡y−cosh⁡xcosh⁡y
c
cosh⁡(x−y)=2cosh⁡xcosh⁡y
d
cosh⁡(x−y)=−2cosh⁡xcosh⁡y
e
cosh⁡(x−y)=cosh⁡xcosh⁡y−sinh⁡xsinh⁡y
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

  1. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

  2. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity: cos⁡(x−y)=cos⁡xcos⁡y+sin⁡xsin⁡y

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is cosh⁡(x−y)=cosh⁡xcosh⁡y−sinh⁡xsinh⁡y.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Deriving a Hyperbolic Identity Using Osborn's Rule
last_observation.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,-\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y.
$$
