observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that  the sample covariance matrix is given by

$$
C=\frac{1}{n-1}B{B}^{T},
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations.

So, we first need to compute the mean-deviation form of our observation matrix.

The sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}15 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sample covariance matrix is 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{3-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 42\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
X=[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & 5 \\ -3 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the observation matrix $X$ above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the sample covariance matrix of the data.
question.worked_solution:
Recall that  the sample covariance matrix is given by

$$
C=\frac{1}{n-1}B{B}^{T},
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations.

So, we first need to compute the mean-deviation form of our observation matrix.

The sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}15 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sample covariance matrix is 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{3-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 42\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

X=[465−306] Consider the observation matrix X above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the sample covariance matrix of the data.

a
12[033−10]
b
12[255−10]
c
12[23342]
d
12[05542]
e
12[03342]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the sample covariance matrix is given by

C=1n−1BBT,

where B is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and n is the number of observations.

So, we first need to compute the mean-deviation form of our observation matrix.

The sample mean is

m=13(x1+x2+x3)=13([4−3]+[60]+[56])=13[153]=[51].

Now, we have the following:

b1=x1−m=[4−3]−[51]=[−1−4]b2=x2−m=[60]−[51]=[1−1]b3=x3−m=[56]−[51]=[05]

Therefore, the mean-deviation form is

B=[−110−4−15].

Finally, the sample covariance matrix is

C=13−1[−110−4−15][−1−41−105]=12[23342].

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
$$
X=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 3 \\ 7 & 5 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the observation matrix $X$ above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the mean-deviation form of $X.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & ⋯ & {x}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

is given by 

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & ⋯ & {b}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

where ${b}_{i}={x}_{i}-m$ for $i=1,2,…,n,$ and $m$ is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that  

$$
{x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}].
$$

As a result, the sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 21\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 1
?

X=[2−23759] Consider the observation matrix X above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the mean-deviation form of X.

a
[0−32122]
b
[−1−120−22]
c
[02−20−22]
d
[1−320−22]
e
[10200−2]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

X=[|||x1x2⋯xn|||]

is given by

B=[|||b1b2⋯bn|||]

where bi=xi−m for i=1,2,…,n, and m is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that

x1=[27],x2=[−25],x3=[39].

As a result, the sample mean is

m=13(x1+x2+x3)=13([27]+[−25]+[39])=13[321]=[17].

Now, we have the following:

b1=x1−m=[27]−[17]=[10]b2=x2−m=[−25]−[17]=[−3−2]b3=x3−m=[39]−[17]=[22]

Therefore, the mean-deviation form is

B=[1−320−22].

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & ⋯ & {x}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

is given by 

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & ⋯ & {b}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

where ${b}_{i}={x}_{i}-m$ for $i=1,2,…,n,$ and $m$ is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that  

$$
{x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}].
$$

As a result, the sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 21\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

X=[|||x1x2⋯xn|||]

is given by

B=[|||b1b2⋯bn|||]

where bi=xi−m for i=1,2,…,n, and m is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that

x1=[27],x2=[−25],x3=[39].

As a result, the sample mean is

m=13(x1+x2+x3)=13([27]+[−25]+[39])=13[321]=[17].

Now, we have the following:

b1=x1−m=[27]−[17]=[10]b2=x2−m=[−25]−[17]=[−3−2]b3=x3−m=[39]−[17]=[22]

Therefore, the mean-deviation form is

B=[1−320−22].

feedback.problem:
$$
X=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 3 \\ 7 & 5 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the observation matrix $X$ above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the mean-deviation form of $X.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & ⋯ & {x}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

is given by 

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & ⋯ & {b}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

where ${b}_{i}={x}_{i}-m$ for $i=1,2,…,n,$ and $m$ is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that  

$$
{x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}].
$$

As a result, the sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 21\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
X=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 & 2 \\ 7 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the observation matrix $X$ above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the mean-deviation form of $X.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & ⋯ & {x}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

is given by 

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & ⋯ & {b}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

where ${b}_{i}={x}_{i}-m$ for $i=1,2,…,n,$ and $m$ is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that  

$$
{x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

As a result, the sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 2
?

X=[−5−32750] Consider the observation matrix X above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the mean-deviation form of X.

a
[−3−1431−4]
b
[01−1−2−13]
c
[11−21−10]
d
[01−2−314]
e
[−312−2−13]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

X=[|||x1x2⋯xn|||]

is given by

B=[|||b1b2⋯bn|||]

where bi=xi−m for i=1,2,…,n, and m is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that

x1=[−57],x2=[−35],x3=[20].

As a result, the sample mean is

m=13(x1+x2+x3)=13([−57]+[−35]+[20])=13[−612]=[−24].

Now, we have the following:

b1=x1−m=[−57]−[−24]=[−33]b2=x2−m=[−35]−[−24]=[−11]b3=x3−m=[20]−[−24]=[4−4]

Therefore, the mean-deviation form is

B=[−3−1431−4].

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & ⋯ & {x}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

is given by 

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & ⋯ & {b}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

where ${b}_{i}={x}_{i}-m$ for $i=1,2,…,n,$ and $m$ is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that  

$$
{x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

As a result, the sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
X=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 & 2 \\ 7 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the observation matrix $X$ above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the mean-deviation form of $X.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & ⋯ & {x}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

is given by 

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & ⋯ & {b}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

where ${b}_{i}={x}_{i}-m$ for $i=1,2,…,n,$ and $m$ is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that  

$$
{x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

As a result, the sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

X=[|||x1x2⋯xn|||]

where bi=xi−m for i=1,2,…,n, and m is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that

x1=[−57],x2=[−35],x3=[20].

As a result, the sample mean is

m=13(x1+x2+x3)=13([−57]+[−35]+[20])=13[−612]=[−24].

Now, we have the following:

b1=x1−m=[−57]−[−24]=[−33]b2=x2−m=[−35]−[−24]=[−11]b3=x3−m=[20]−[−24]=[4−4]

Therefore, the mean-deviation form is

Question 2
?

X=[−5−32750] Consider the observation matrix X above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the mean-deviation form of X.

a
[−3−1431−4]
b
[01−1−2−13]
c
[11−21−10]
d
[01−2−314]
e
[−312−2−13]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

X=[|||x1x2⋯xn|||]

is given by

B=[|||b1b2⋯bn|||]

where bi=xi−m for i=1,2,…,n, and m is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that

x1=[−57],x2=[−35],x3=[20].

As a result, the sample mean is

m=13(x1+x2+x3)=13([−57]+[−35]+[20])=13[−612]=[−24].

Now, we have the following:

b1=x1−m=[−57]−[−24]=[−33]b2=x2−m=[−35]−[−24]=[−11]b3=x3−m=[20]−[−24]=[4−4]

Therefore, the mean-deviation form is

B=[−3−1431−4].

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
B=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the observation matrix $B$ in the mean-deviation form above, where the individual observations are given in columns. 
Find the sample covariance matrix of the data.
question.worked_solution:
Recall that  the sample covariance matrix is given by

$$
C=\frac{1}{n-1}B{B}^{T},
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{4-1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}10 & 2 \\ 2 & 42\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

B=[2−11−205−1−4] Consider the observation matrix B in the mean-deviation form above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the sample covariance matrix of the data.

a
13[3477−29]
b
13[46777721]
c
13[34−17−17−29]
d
13[102242]
e
13[1200−27]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the sample covariance matrix is given by

C=1n−1BBT,

where B is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and n is the number of observations.

Therefore, we obtain

C=14−1[2−11−205−1−4][20−151−1−2−4]=13[102242].

EXPLANATION

Recall that the sample covariance matrix is given by

C=1n−1BBT,

where B is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and n is the number of observations.

Therefore, we obtain

C=14−1[2−11−205−1−4][20−151−1−2−4]=13[102242].

solution.reasoning: There are four observations, so the sample covariance is BB^T/(4-1). The diagonal entries of BB^T are 2^2+(-1)^2+1^2+(-2)^2=10 and 0^2+5^2+(-1)^2+(-4)^2=42. The off-diagonal entry is 2(0)+(-1)(5)+1(-1)+(-2)(-4)=2. Thus option d is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.worked_solution:

$$
C=\frac{1}{n-1}B{B}^{T},

Therefore, we obtain

$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 & -6 & 1 \\ 10 & -6 & 5 & -9\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the observation matrix $B$ in the mean-deviation form above, where the individual observations are given in columns. 
Find the sample covariance matrix of the data.
question.worked_solution:
Recall that  the sample covariance matrix is given by

$$
C=\frac{1}{n-1}B{B}^{T},
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{4-1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 & -6 & 1 \\ 10 & -6 & 5 & -9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 10 \\ 5 & -6 \\ -6 & 5 \\ 1 & -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}62 & -69 \\ -69 & 242\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

B=[05−6110−65−9] Consider the observation matrix B in the mean-deviation form above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the sample covariance matrix of the data.

a
13[300069]
b
13[62−69−69242]
c
13[523030250]
d
13[6500340]
e
13[25−25−2547]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the sample covariance matrix is given by

C=1n−1BBT,

where B is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and n is the number of observations.

Therefore, we obtain

C=14−1[05−6110−65−9][0105−6−651−9]=13[62−69−69242].

EXPLANATION

Recall that the sample covariance matrix is given by

C=1n−1BBT,

where B is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and n is the number of observations.

Therefore, we obtain

C=14−1[05−6110−65−9][0105−6−651−9]=13[62−69−69242].

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
X=[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & 5 \\ -3 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the observation matrix $X$ above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the sample covariance matrix of the data.
question.worked_solution:
Recall that  the sample covariance matrix is given by

$$
C=\frac{1}{n-1}B{B}^{T},
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations.

So, we first need to compute the mean-deviation form of our observation matrix.

The sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}15 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sample covariance matrix is 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{3-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 42\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

X=[465−306] Consider the observation matrix X above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the sample covariance matrix of the data.

a
12[033−10]
b
12[255−10]
c
12[23342]
d
12[05542]
e
12[03342]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the sample covariance matrix is given by

C=1n−1BBT,

where B is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and n is the number of observations.

So, we first need to compute the mean-deviation form of our observation matrix.

The sample mean is

m=13(x1+x2+x3)=13([4−3]+[60]+[56])=13[153]=[51].

Now, we have the following:

b1=x1−m=[4−3]−[51]=[−1−4]b2=x2−m=[60]−[51]=[1−1]b3=x3−m=[56]−[51]=[05]

Therefore, the mean-deviation form is

B=[−110−4−15].

Finally, the sample covariance matrix is

C=13−1[−110−4−15][−1−41−105]=12[23342].

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that  the sample covariance matrix is given by

$$
C=\frac{1}{n-1}B{B}^{T},
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations.

So, we first need to compute the mean-deviation form of our observation matrix.

The sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}15 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sample covariance matrix is 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{3-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 42\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

X=[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & 5 \\ -3 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

X=[465−306] Consider the observation matrix X above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the sample covariance matrix of the data.

a
12[033−10]
b
12[255−10]
c
12[23342]
d
12[05542]
e
12[03342]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the sample covariance matrix is given by

C=1n−1BBT,

where B is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and n is the number of observations.

So, we first need to compute the mean-deviation form of our observation matrix.

The sample mean is

m=13(x1+x2+x3)=13([4−3]+[60]+[56])=13[153]=[51].

Now, we have the following:

b1=x1−m=[4−3]−[51]=[−1−4]b2=x2−m=[60]−[51]=[1−1]b3=x3−m=[56]−[51]=[05]

Therefore, the mean-deviation form is

B=[−110−4−15].

Finally, the sample covariance matrix is

C=13−1[−110−4−15][−1−41−105]=12[23342].

solution.reasoning: The mean observation is (5,1)^T, so the centered rows are (-1,1,0) and (-4,-1,5). Their squared norms are 2 and 42, and their dot product is 4-1=3. Dividing the resulting matrix by n-1=2 gives option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
$$
X=[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & 5 \\ -3 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the observation matrix $X$ above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the sample covariance matrix of the data.
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that  the sample covariance matrix is given by

$$
C=\frac{1}{n-1}B{B}^{T},
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations.

So, we first need to compute the mean-deviation form of our observation matrix.

The sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}15 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sample covariance matrix is 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{3-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 42\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the identity for $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}):$

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}
$$

Using $x=\theta $ in the above identity, the integral can be rewritten as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={2\cdot 2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4(1-0) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2})(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1))-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)-2\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(x)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1))-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1))(1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)-2(-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+D) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)-2D \\  & =({x}^{2}-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2D.$

questions.worked_solution:
To find when the total amount is a minimum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=0.$ First, we differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1500+{\int }_{0}^{t}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1500)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({\int }_{0}^{t}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{0}^{t}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{t}^{2}-27\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve $\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=0$:

$$
3{t}^{2}-27=0\,⇒\,t=3
$$

So there are two candidates for global extrema, $t=0$ and $t=3.$ To find out how much money is in the account when $t=3,$ we figure out $M(3)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}M(3) & =1500+{\int }_{0}^{3}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x \\  & =1500+[{x}^{3}-27x]{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =1500+[({3}^{3}-27(3))-(0)] \\  & =1500+[27-81] \\  & =1500-54 \\  & =1446\end{aligned}
$$

Since $1446<1500$, we conclude that the minimum amount is $$\,1446$, and this will happen after $3$ days.

questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1-x} & =0 \\ 1-x & =0 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{1-x})=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-x}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4(1-x)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{\frac{5-4x}{4(1-x)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{\frac{4x-5}{x-1}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

4.Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of X?

Consider the arc of the curve y=1−x that lies in the first quadrant between x=0 and its x-intercept. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

questions.worked_solution:
Since the growth rate of vaccinated people is *jointly* proportional to the number of people who have been vaccinated at time $t,$ and the number of unvaccinated people, the number of vaccinated people follows a logistic growth model.

A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.3,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=50\,000\,000.$ Therefore, the number of people who have been vaccinated is given by the equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.3P(50\,000\,000-P).
$$

questions.raw_html:
5.Constructing a Logistic Growth Equation?

A population of 50000000 people is being vaccinated against a disease. The rate of growth in the number of people P(t) vaccinated is jointly proportional to the number of people who have been vaccinated at time t, measured in months, and the number of unvaccinated people. If the constant of proportionality is 0.3, which differential equation could be used to model P(t)?

e

solution.reasoning: M(t)=1500+t^3-27t, so M'(t)=3(t-3)(t+3). For t≥0, M decreases until t=3 and increases thereafter, giving its global minimum at 3 days. M(3)=1500+27-81=1446 dollars. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was supplied.

$$

where $M$ is measured in dollars, and $t\ge 0$ is the time (in days) since the first day of the campaign.

feedback.worked_solution:
To find when the total amount is a minimum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=0.$ First, we differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1500+{\int }_{0}^{t}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1500)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({\int }_{0}^{t}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{0}^{t}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{t}^{2}-27\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve $\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=0$:

$$
3{t}^{2}-27=0\,⇒\,t=3
$$

So there are two candidates for global extrema, $t=0$ and $t=3.$ To find out how much money is in the account when $t=3,$ we figure out $M(3)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}M(3) & =1500+{\int }_{0}^{3}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x \\  & =1500+[{x}^{3}-27x]{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =1500+[({3}^{3}-27(3))-(0)] \\  & =1500+[27-81] \\  & =1500-54 \\  & =1446\end{aligned}
$$

Since $1446<1500$, we conclude that the minimum amount is $$\,1446$, and this will happen after $3$ days.

Question 4

Consider the arc of the curve y=1−x that lies in the first quadrant between x=0 and its x-intercept. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
 π∫01x4x−5x−1dx
b
 2π∫01x4x−7x−1dx
c
 π∫02x2x−1dx
d
 2π∫01xx−1dx
e
 π∫024x−7x−1dx

question.html:
Question 4

Consider the arc of the curve y=1−x that lies in the first quadrant between x=0 and its x-intercept. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
 π∫01x4x−5x−1dx
b
 2π∫01x4x−7x−1dx
c
 π∫02x2x−1dx
d
 2π∫01xx−1dx
e
 π∫024x−7x−1dx

solution.reasoning: Rotation about the y-axis gives S=2\pi\int_0^1 x\sqrt{1+(y')^2}\,dx. Since y'=-1/(2\sqrt{1-x}), this simplifies to \pi\int_0^1 x\sqrt{(5-4x)/(1-x)}\,dx, which equals option a because (5-4x)/(1-x)=(4x-5)/(x-1). The integral is improper but convergent at x=1. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was supplied.

question.problem: A population of $50\,000\,000$ people is being vaccinated against a disease. The rate of growth in the number of people $P(t)$ vaccinated is jointly proportional to the number of people who have been vaccinated at time $t,$ measured in months, and the number of unvaccinated people. If the constant of proportionality is $0.3,$ which differential equation could be used to model $P(t)?$

question.html:
Question 5

A population of 50000000 people is being vaccinated against a disease. The rate of growth in the number of people P(t) vaccinated is jointly proportional to the number of people who have been vaccinated at time t, measured in months, and the number of unvaccinated people. If the constant of proportionality is 0.3, which differential equation could be used to model P(t)?

a
 dPdt=0.3P(50000000−P)
b
 dPdt=0.3P(50000000+P)
c
 dPdt=50000000P(0.3−P)
d
 dPdt=50000000P(0.3+P)
e
 dPdt=−0.3P(50000000−P)

question.problem: A population of $50\,000\,000$ people is being vaccinated against a disease. The rate of growth in the number of people $P(t)$ vaccinated is jointly proportional to the number of people who have been vaccinated at time $t,$ measured in months, and the number of unvaccinated people. If the constant of proportionality is $0.3,$ which differential equation could be used to model $P(t)?$

question.html:
Question 5

A population of 50000000 people is being vaccinated against a disease. The rate of growth in the number of people P(t) vaccinated is jointly proportional to the number of people who have been vaccinated at time t, measured in months, and the number of unvaccinated people. If the constant of proportionality is 0.3, which differential equation could be used to model P(t)?

a
 dPdt=0.3P(50000000−P)
b
 dPdt=0.3P(50000000+P)
c
 dPdt=50000000P(0.3−P)
d
 dPdt=50000000P(0.3+P)
e
 dPdt=−0.3P(50000000−P)

solution.reasoning: There are P vaccinated people and 50,000,000-P unvaccinated people. Joint proportionality with positive constant 0.3 gives dP/dt=0.3P(50,000,000-P), option a. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was supplied.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/e679efaa2612d45bbfe8b918de7148853b64eaf530af34a525ef1735e0946b09.png)

Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive

II. The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero

III. The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. From the diagram below it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/fbcd6fd0fadcc955212a145de9edb4654ddb92ddebb8ba31eb775cff676efeeb.png)

Therefore, the flux is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

- Statement III is true. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/a3d398d382e6bc94ddde77e650d50a6b5ec050083f89f64104f6f2fd172a9239.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. From the diagram below it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/6b24ece279cc480f20d7a4dbc65f7a5257af71f22688b1416c73e3b40673a321.png)

Therefore, the flux is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

- Statement III is true. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/9e8527d26f0f2bd5372d8643f8f9321ec022bb0079e1fc5b23be4978f436613c.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = 8y\,\mathbf i + 4x\,\mathbf j$ and the circle $C$ given by $x^2+y^2 = 4.$ If the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/9d24a5f692535453b1b34c2bc9236bd44cd2c88c05724a2a5dbdf804b98957e5.svg)

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ is $\mathbf n = \dfrac x2\,\mathbf i + \dfrac y2\,\mathbf j.$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/ff84680c55f5349431cf3d70066eeaba2c680569faa3b2210e5d14ef63ccd99e.png)

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}(8y\,i+4x\,j)\cdot (\frac{x}{2}i+\frac{y}{2}\,j)\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{C}4xy+2xy\,\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{C}6xy\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is $6xy.$

Example: 
                    Calculating Flux Across a Square Using Symmetry
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/05c91d681a0c84bbe9d8b6cab9bd8cdf1dca8bf88c851b8c7a7045f73ff9844c.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F = 2x\,\mathbf i + 2y\,\mathbf j$ and a square $C$ with side length $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/1de4c4c55784b4a84a0493a4cc65082c430cadcc39c3d808001b2fd27665e968.png)

First, consider the side $C_1.$ We have that $\mathbf n_1 = \mathbf i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(2x\,i+2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \mathbf i + t\,\mathbf j, \quad \Rightarrow\quad \mathbf r'(t) = \mathbf j, \qquad t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =2(1-(-1)) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides $C_2, C_3,$ and $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 4\cdot 4 = 16.
$$

Example: 
                    Calculating Flux Across a Rectangle Using Two Symmetry Properties
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/59b5f1676f036f80e6aa2e9e331327ed9ec28e88bacda52a91ee0865736e9ce3.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F = 5x\,\mathbf i - 3y\,\mathbf j$ and a rectangle $C$ with base $4$ and height $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$ 

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/793755cda5243dbb427d8722c21ab150a4821c3957f0ccd0ef0fedbbd576e924.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side $C_1.$ We have that $\mathbf n_1 = \mathbf i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(5x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =5{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = 2\mathbf i + t\,\mathbf j, \quad \Rightarrow\quad \mathbf r'(t) = \mathbf j, \qquad t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =5{\int }_{-1}^{1}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =10{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =10\cdot 2 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_3$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s = 20.
$$

- Next, we consider the side $C_2.$ We have that $\mathbf n_2 = \mathbf j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(5x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_2,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = t\,\mathbf i + \mathbf j, \quad \Rightarrow\quad \mathbf r'(t) = \mathbf i, \qquad t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-3{\int }_{-2}^{2}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =(-3)\cdot 4 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = -12.
$$

Finally, then

$$
\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s= 2 \cdot 20 + 2 \cdot (-12) = 16.
$$

tutorials.name: Constructing an Integral Formula for the Flux
tutorials.problem:
If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png)

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png)

Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png)

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png)

Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

tutorials.name: Calculating Flux
tutorials.problem:
To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

 

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$

tutorials.name: Using  Symmetry to Simplify Flux Calculations
tutorials.problem:
Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry.

To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png)

If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png)

Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

This is easy to verify, since, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ 

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
=
-\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
Let $\mathbf F$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. Imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water, and $C$ is a curve that allows water to flow through it (like a fishing net). 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol C$** is a scalar number that tells us how much water is escaping the region bounded by $C.$ 

We have three possible scenarios: 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/6ff4d006d3fbf4a434f35a13c8591fc166ff6c74adf2b7969752b7541e486df2.png)

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/3812148e855a84e3233316acc8bbf59bd7cd802a874c9e4807c6efd7ca6754cf.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

The following vector field has zero flux across $C$ because the amount of water flowing in through $C$ equals the amount of water flowing out through $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/56aef4f217e9981755826745a97e8389d86b49518ffd7d3ebc75e5ee2dc28f8b.png)

The following two vector fields also have a zero flux across $C$ because the water flow is tangential to $C$ at every point along $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/637677324152af3d428e405c89025f35dbe5d71e2e8f0a0797ef3aca30bae7e1.png)

If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

$$

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is also positive, and we have

$$
\oint\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0.
$$

$$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C\mathbin:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

The outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. From the diagram below we see that $\mathbf F$ acts perpendicular to $\mathbf n$ at every point on $C.$ Therefore, there is no net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/4a3d9864bb6bada1fd218b299427bc5bb4ffcbcccb1a504fff77416d5d292151.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

- Statement III is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/9310d17389f61de2984c0e23cfe1060e77d4a87a140d2f1c892bdbab9b99629b.png)

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/e679efaa2612d45bbfe8b918de7148853b64eaf530af34a525ef1735e0946b09.png)

Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive

II. The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero

III. The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive
question.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. From the diagram below it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/fbcd6fd0fadcc955212a145de9edb4654ddb92ddebb8ba31eb775cff676efeeb.png)

Therefore, the flux is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

- Statement III is true. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223345/assets/a3d398d382e6bc94ddde77e650d50a6b5ec050083f89f64104f6f2fd172a9239.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Evaluate $1+(2-3x)$ for $x=-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We replace $x$ with $-1$ in the expression and evaluate the parentheses first:

$$
\begin{aligned}1+(2-3x) & = \\ 1+(2-3\cdot (-1)) & = \\ 1+(2-(-3)) & = \\ 1+(2+3) & = \\ 1+5 & = \\ 6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $p=2$ and $q=-2,$ then $8p+7q+2=$
questions.worked_solution:
Replacing $p$ with $2$ and $q$ with $-2$ in the expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8p+7q+2 & = \\ 8(2)+7(-2)+2 & = \\ 16+(-14)+2 & = \\ 16-14+2 & = \\ 4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that $∇f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡y\,i+\frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}\,j$ and $r(t)=({t}^{2}+1)\,i+t\,j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡y\,i+\frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x={t}^{2}+1$ and $y=t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =2t\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+j)\cdot (2t\,i+j) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\cdot 2t+1\cdot 1 \\  & =2t\operatorname{arctan}⁡t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =2(1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+1 \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+1 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},2t-1⟩$ at the point $t=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2x,-2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=2t-1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2{t}^{2},-2(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},2-4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},2-4t⟩\cdot ⟨2t,2⟩ \\  & =2{t}^{2}\cdot 2t+(2-4t)\cdot 2 \\  & =4{t}^{3}-8t+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(0))] & =4(0)^{3}-8(0)+4 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\sqrt{t},3t-1⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t,y=\sqrt{t}$ and $z=3t-1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\sqrt{t}(3t-1),2t(3t-1),2t\sqrt{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨(3t-1)\sqrt{t},6{t}^{2}-2t,2t\sqrt{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨(3t-1)\sqrt{t},6{t}^{2}-2t,2t\sqrt{t}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},3⟩ \\  & =(3t-1)\sqrt{t}\cdot 2+(6{t}^{2}-2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+2t\sqrt{t}\cdot 3 \\  & =6t\sqrt{t}-2\sqrt{t}+\frac{3{t}^{2}-t}{\sqrt{t}}+6t\sqrt{t} \\  & =12t\sqrt{t}-2\sqrt{t}+\frac{3{t}^{2}-t}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =12(1)\sqrt{1}-2\sqrt{1}+\frac{3(1)^{2}-1}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)=yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,k \\  & =-yz\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,i+z\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y={e}^{t},$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}\,i+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =2t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}\,i+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,k)\cdot (2t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot {e}^{t}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}+2{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}-t\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)$ and $r(t)=t\,i+2t\,j+\frac{1}{t}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,k \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,i+xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,j+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y=2t$ and $z=\frac{1}{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k)\cdot (\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 2+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2x,-2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=2t-1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2{t}^{2},-2(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},2-4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},2-4t⟩\cdot ⟨2t,2⟩ \\  & =2{t}^{2}\cdot 2t+(2-4t)\cdot 2 \\  & =4{t}^{3}-8t+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(0))] & =4(0)^{3}-8(0)+4 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$
