question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223065/assets/f531f2467284ef84e0af0758a8e8554f1e5f72ea08d30d0b80c83076fbe5d7a3.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(x+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,0)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(0+t(1-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+t)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & =1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[t+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(0+\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}

Evaluate ∫C(x+πcos⁡πy)dx, where C is the path traversed along the line segment from the point (1,0) to the point (2,1), as shown above.

EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dxdtdt.

The curve C is a line segment with endpoints (1,0) and (2,1). It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨(1+t(2−1)),(0+t(1−0))⟩=⟨1+t,t⟩, where 0≤t≤1.

Computing dxdt, we get the following:

dxdt=ddt(1+t)=1

Now, since f(x,y)=x+πcos⁡πy, we obtain

f(r(t))=(1+t)+πcos⁡πt=1+t+πcos⁡πt.

We can now evaluate the integral:

∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫01f(r(t))dxdtdt=∫01(1+t+πcos⁡πt)⋅1⋅dt=∫011+t+πcos⁡πtdt=[t+t22+sin⁡πt]01=(1+122+sin⁡π)−(0+sin⁡0)=32

last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,0)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(0+t(1-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+t)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & =1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[t+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(0+\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Evaluate ∫C(x+πcos⁡πy)dx, where C is the path traversed along the line segment from the point (1,0) to the point (2,1), as shown above.

a
52
b
2
c
1
d
32
e
12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dxdtdt.

The curve C is a line segment with endpoints (1,0) and (2,1). It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨(1+t(2−1)),(0+t(1−0))⟩=⟨1+t,t⟩, where 0≤t≤1.

Computing dxdt, we get the following:

dxdt=ddt(1+t)=1

Now, since f(x,y)=x+πcos⁡πy, we obtain

f(r(t))=(1+t)+πcos⁡πt=1+t+πcos⁡πt.

We can now evaluate the integral:

∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫01f(r(t))dxdtdt=∫01(1+t+πcos⁡πt)⋅1⋅dt=∫011+t+πcos⁡πtdt=[t+t22+sin⁡πt]01=(1+122+sin⁡π)−(0+sin⁡0)=32

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223065/assets/36b985c811eb28d8220017c6b7407b3a104554d785dafdb35f17553c262bdc35.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-2)$ to the point $(2,4),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩.$*
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-2)$ and $(2,4).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-2+t(4-(-2)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)\cdot (6t-2) \\  & =18{t}^{2}-12t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18{t}^{2}-12t+2)\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-6t+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-2)$ and $(2,4).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-2+t(4-(-2)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)\cdot (6t-2) \\  & =18{t}^{2}-12t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18{t}^{2}-12t+2)\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-6t+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxydy, where C is the path along the line segment from the point (−1,−2) to the point (2,4), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨3t−1,6t−2⟩.

a
18∫01(t2+6t+9)dt
b
18∫01(t2−6t+9)dt
c
6∫01(9t2−6t+1)dt
d
12∫01(t2−6t+9)dt
e
12∫01(9t2−6t+1)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C is a line segment with endpoints (−1,−2) and (2,4). It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨(−1+t(2−(−1))),(−2+t(4−(−2)))⟩=⟨3t−1,6t−2⟩, where 0≤t≤1.

Computing dydt, we get the following:

dydt=ddt(6t−2)=6

Now, since f(x,y)=xy, we obtain

f(r(t))=(3t−1)⋅(6t−2)=18t2−12t+2.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫01f(r(t))dydtdt=∫01(18t2−12t+2)⋅6⋅dt=12∫01(9t2−6t+1)dt.

solution.reasoning: For 0≤t≤1, x=3t−1, y=6t−2=2(3t−1), and dy=6dt. Therefore xy dy=12(3t−1)²dt=12(9t²−6t+1)dt, giving option e. No captured Math Academy answer or grading evidence establishes its stated key.

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223065/assets/36b985c811eb28d8220017c6b7407b3a104554d785dafdb35f17553c262bdc35.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-2)$ to the point $(2,4),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩.$*
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-2)$ and $(2,4).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-2+t(4-(-2)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)\cdot (6t-2) \\  & =18{t}^{2}-12t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18{t}^{2}-12t+2)\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-6t+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxydy, where C is the path along the line segment from the point (−1,−2) to the point (2,4), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨3t−1,6t−2⟩.

a
18∫01(t2+6t+9)dt
b
18∫01(t2−6t+9)dt
c
6∫01(9t2−6t+1)dt
d
12∫01(t2−6t+9)dt
e
12∫01(9t2−6t+1)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C is a line segment with endpoints (−1,−2) and (2,4). It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨(−1+t(2−(−1))),(−2+t(4−(−2)))⟩=⟨3t−1,6t−2⟩, where 0≤t≤1.

Computing dydt, we get the following:

dydt=ddt(6t−2)=6

Now, since f(x,y)=xy, we obtain

f(r(t))=(3t−1)⋅(6t−2)=18t2−12t+2.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫01f(r(t))dydtdt=∫01(18t2−12t+2)⋅6⋅dt=12∫01(9t2−6t+1)dt.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223065/assets/ab95b870025708090e40cbd7645072e8f4453cf50047b2a00036a30171c81994.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(\sqrt{x-1}+y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(1,2)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,2)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(2+t(1-2))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,2-t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x-1}+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sqrt{(1+t)-1}+2-t \\  & =\sqrt{t}-t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{t}-t+2)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{1/2}-t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+2t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+2)-(0) \\  & =\frac{13}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ∫C(x−1+y)dx, where C is the path traversed along the line segment from the point (1,2) to the point (2,1), as shown above.

EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫abf(r(t))dxdtdt.

The curve C is a line segment with endpoints (1,2) and (2,1). It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨(1+t(2−1)),(2+t(1−2))⟩=⟨1+t,2−t⟩, where 0≤t≤1.

Computing dxdt, we get the following:

dxdt=ddt(1+t)=1

Now, since f(x,y)=x−1+y, we obtain

f(r(t))=(1+t)−1+2−t=t−t+2.

We can now evaluate the integral:

∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫01f(r(t))dxdtdt=∫01(t−t+2)⋅1⋅dt=∫01(t1/2−t+2)dt=[2t3/23−t22+2t]01=(23−12+2)−(0)=136

last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,2)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(2+t(1-2))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,2-t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x-1}+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sqrt{(1+t)-1}+2-t \\  & =\sqrt{t}-t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{t}-t+2)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{1/2}-t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+2t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+2)-(0) \\  & =\frac{13}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3

Evaluate ∫C(x−1+y)dx, where C is the path traversed along the line segment from the point (1,2) to the point (2,1), as shown above.

EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫abf(r(t))dxdtdt.

The curve C is a line segment with endpoints (1,2) and (2,1). It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨(1+t(2−1)),(2+t(1−2))⟩=⟨1+t,2−t⟩, where 0≤t≤1.

Computing dxdt, we get the following:

dxdt=ddt(1+t)=1

Now, since f(x,y)=x−1+y, we obtain

f(r(t))=(1+t)−1+2−t=t−t+2.

We can now evaluate the integral:

∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫01f(r(t))dxdtdt=∫01(t−t+2)⋅1⋅dt=∫01(t1/2−t+2)dt=[2t3/23−t22+2t]01=(23−12+2)−(0)=136

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223065/assets/f83043b44a8ad9181e66de57357397deb49c4b0e79b5e6e16330305a58391148.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(4,0)$ to the point $(-4,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxydy, where C is the path along a circle of radius 4, traversed from the point (4,0) to the point (−4,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
16∫0π(sin⁡t+cos2⁡t)dt
b
64∫0π(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)dt
c
64∫0πsin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
d
 32∫0πsin⁡tcos⁡tdt
e
 4∫0πsin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 4 centered at O. It can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,0≤t≤π.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(4sin⁡t)=4cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=xy, we obtain f(r(t))=(4cos⁡t)(4sin⁡t)=16sin⁡tcos⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫0πf(r(t))dydtdt=∫0π16sin⁡tcos⁡t⋅4cos⁡tdt=64∫0πsin⁡tcos2⁡tdt.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxydy, where C is the path along a circle of radius 4, traversed from the point (4,0) to the point (−4,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
16∫0π(sin⁡t+cos2⁡t)dt
b
64∫0π(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)dt
c
64∫0πsin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
d
 32∫0πsin⁡tcos⁡tdt
e
 4∫0πsin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 4 centered at O. It can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,0≤t≤π.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(4sin⁡t)=4cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=xy, we obtain f(r(t))=(4cos⁡t)(4sin⁡t)=16sin⁡tcos⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫0πf(r(t))dydtdt=∫0π16sin⁡tcos⁡t⋅4cos⁡tdt=64∫0πsin⁡tcos2⁡tdt.

solution.reasoning: The upper semicircle corresponds to 0≤t≤π. Substituting x=4cos(t), y=4sin(t), and dy=4cos(t)dt gives xy dy=64sin(t)cos²(t)dt, so option c is equivalent. No captured Math Academy answer or grading evidence establishes its stated key.

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223065/assets/f83043b44a8ad9181e66de57357397deb49c4b0e79b5e6e16330305a58391148.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(4,0)$ to the point $(-4,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxydy, where C is the path along a circle of radius 4, traversed from the point (4,0) to the point (−4,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
16∫0π(sin⁡t+cos2⁡t)dt
b
64∫0π(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)dt
c
64∫0πsin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
d
 32∫0πsin⁡tcos⁡tdt
e
 4∫0πsin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 4 centered at O. It can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,0≤t≤π.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(4sin⁡t)=4cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=xy, we obtain f(r(t))=(4cos⁡t)(4sin⁡t)=16sin⁡tcos⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫0πf(r(t))dydtdt=∫0π16sin⁡tcos⁡t⋅4cos⁡tdt=64∫0πsin⁡tcos2⁡tdt.

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=64,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =12{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12 \\  & =4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(3x2+y2)dy, where C is the path along the ellipse 16x2+4y2=64, traversed from the point (−2,0) to the point (2,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos⁡tdt
b
4∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos2⁡tdt
c
16∫π2π(3sin2⁡t+1)cos⁡tdt
d
8∫π2π(3sin2⁡t+1)sin⁡tdt
e
16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)sin2⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,π≤t≤2π.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(4sin⁡t)=4cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=3x2+y2, we obtain f(r(t))=3(2cos⁡t)2+(4sin⁡t)2=12cos2⁡t+16sin2⁡t=4sin2⁡t+12(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=4sin2⁡t+12=4(sin2⁡t+3).

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫π2πf(r(t))dydtdt=∫π2π4(sin2⁡t+3)⋅4cos⁡tdt=16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos⁡tdt.

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =12{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12 \\  & =4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(3x2+y2)dy, where C is the path along the ellipse 16x2+4y2=64, traversed from the point (−2,0) to the point (2,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos⁡tdt
b
4∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos2⁡tdt
c
16∫π2π(3sin2⁡t+1)cos⁡tdt
d
8∫π2π(3sin2⁡t+1)sin⁡tdt
e
16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)sin2⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,π≤t≤2π.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(4sin⁡t)=4cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=3x2+y2, we obtain f(r(t))=3(2cos⁡t)2+(4sin⁡t)2=12cos2⁡t+16sin2⁡t=4sin2⁡t+12(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=4sin2⁡t+12=4(sin2⁡t+3).

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫π2πf(r(t))dydtdt=∫π2π4(sin2⁡t+3)⋅4cos⁡tdt=16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos⁡tdt.

solution.reasoning: The lower half corresponds to π≤t≤2π. Substitution gives (3x²+y²)dy=(12cos²t+16sin²t)4cos(t)dt=16(sin²t+3)cos(t)dt, exactly option a. Both a and c evaluate to zero, so a is the direct parametrized form but is not uniquely equivalent numerically. No Math Academy key or grade is captured.

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223065/assets/fd1956c8291f1bcecd7d37082110861ed7265fa40f7f85cbc69221cfdc5bea2d.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=64,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =12{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12 \\  & =4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(3x2+y2)dy, where C is the path along the ellipse 16x2+4y2=64, traversed from the point (−2,0) to the point (2,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos⁡tdt
b
4∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos2⁡tdt
c
16∫π2π(3sin2⁡t+1)cos⁡tdt
d
8∫π2π(3sin2⁡t+1)sin⁡tdt
e
16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)sin2⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,π≤t≤2π.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(4sin⁡t)=4cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=3x2+y2, we obtain f(r(t))=3(2cos⁡t)2+(4sin⁡t)2=12cos2⁡t+16sin2⁡t=4sin2⁡t+12(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=4sin2⁡t+12=4(sin2⁡t+3).

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫π2πf(r(t))dydtdt=∫π2π4(sin2⁡t+3)⋅4cos⁡tdt=16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos⁡tdt.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{(2{n}^{2}+3)(2{n}^{2}-3)}{2n(5{n}^{3}-1)}$ for $n\ge 1?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we multiply out the numerator and denominator of the sequence and get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(2{n}^{2}+3)(2{n}^{2}-3)}{2n(5{n}^{3}-1)}=\frac{4{n}^{4}-9}{10{n}^{4}-2n}.
$$

So to find the limit, we will need to compute

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{4{n}^{4}-9}{10{n}^{4}-2n}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $10{n}^{4},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{4}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{4{n}^{4}-9}{10{n}^{4}-2n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{4{n}^{4}}{{n}^{4}}-\frac{9}{{n}^{4}})}{(\frac{10{n}^{4}}{{n}^{4}}-\frac{2n}{{n}^{4}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(4-\frac{9}{{n}^{4}})}{(10-\frac{2}{{n}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{4-0}{10-0} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sequence converges and its limit is $\frac{2}{5}.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{8{n}^{5}-2n}{8{n}^{4}-2}$ for $n\ge 1?$
questions.worked_solution:
The dominant term in the denominator is $8{n}^{4},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{4}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{8{n}^{5}-2n}{8{n}^{4}-2} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{8{n}^{5}}{{n}^{4}}-\frac{2n}{{n}^{4}})}{(\frac{8{n}^{4}}{{n}^{4}}-\frac{2}{{n}^{4}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(8n-\frac{2}{{n}^{3}})}{(8-\frac{2}{{n}^{4}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{8n-0}{8-0} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }n \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The limit does not exist, so the sequence diverges.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{1-{n}^{4}}{3{n}^{2}+5}$ for $n\ge 1?$
questions.worked_solution:
The dominant term  in the denominator is $3{n}^{2}$, so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1-{n}^{4}}{3{n}^{2}+5} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{{n}^{4}}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{3{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}+\frac{5}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}-{n}^{2})}{(3+\frac{5}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{0-{n}^{2}}{3+0} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(-\frac{{n}^{2}}{3}) \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The limit does not exist, so the sequence diverges.

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{(3n-2)(3n+2)}{n(1-9n)}$ for $n\ge 1?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we multiply out the numerator and denominator of the sequence and get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(3n-2)(3n+2)}{n(1-9n)}=\frac{9{n}^{2}-4}{n-9{n}^{2}}.
$$

So to find the limit, we will need to compute

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{9{n}^{2}-4}{n-9{n}^{2}}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $-9{n}^{2},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{9{n}^{2}-4}{n-9{n}^{2}} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{9{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{4}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{n}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{9{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(9-\frac{4}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{1}{n}-9)} \\  & =\frac{9-0}{0-9} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sequence converges and its limit is $-1.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.worked_solution:
To determine whether the sequence converges or diverges, we need to determine the limit of the sequence as $n$ approaches infinity:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{12n+1}{3n}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $3n,$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by $n$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{12n+1}{3n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{12n}{n}+\frac{1}{n})}{\frac{3n}{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{12+\frac{1}{n}}{3} \\  & =\frac{12+0}{3} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sequence converges, and its limit is $4.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

What is the limit of the sequence an=(2n2+3)(2n2−3)2n(5n3−1) for n≥1?

a
0
b
52
c
25
d
The sequence diverges
e
1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we multiply out the numerator and denominator of the sequence and get

an=(2n2+3)(2n2−3)2n(5n3−1)=4n4−910n4−2n.

So to find the limit, we will need to compute limn→∞an=limn→∞4n4−910n4−2n.

The dominant term in the denominator is 10n4, so we divide the numerator and the denominator by n4 and get limn→∞4n4−910n4−2n=limn→∞(4n4n4−9n4)(10n4n4−2nn4)=limn→∞(4−9n4)(10−2n3)=4−010−0=25.

Consequently, the sequence converges and its limit is 25.

$$

question.worked_solution:
The dominant term in the denominator is $8{n}^{4},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{4}$ and get

$$

feedback.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{1-{n}^{4}}{3{n}^{2}+5}$ for $n\ge 1?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The dominant term  in the denominator is $3{n}^{2}$, so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1-{n}^{4}}{3{n}^{2}+5} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{{n}^{4}}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{3{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}+\frac{5}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}-{n}^{2})}{(3+\frac{5}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{0-{n}^{2}}{3+0} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(-\frac{{n}^{2}}{3}) \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The limit does not exist, so the sequence diverges.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{(3n-2)(3n+2)}{n(1-9n)}$ for $n\ge 1?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we multiply out the numerator and denominator of the sequence and get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(3n-2)(3n+2)}{n(1-9n)}=\frac{9{n}^{2}-4}{n-9{n}^{2}}.
$$

So to find the limit, we will need to compute

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{9{n}^{2}-4}{n-9{n}^{2}}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $-9{n}^{2},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{9{n}^{2}-4}{n-9{n}^{2}} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{9{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{4}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{n}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{9{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(9-\frac{4}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{1}{n}-9)} \\  & =\frac{9-0}{0-9} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sequence converges and its limit is $-1.$

EXPLANATION

First, we multiply out the numerator and denominator of the sequence and get

an=(3n−2)(3n+2)n(1−9n)=9n2−4n−9n2.

So to find the limit, we will need to compute

limn→∞an=limn→∞9n2−4n−9n2.

The dominant term in the denominator is −9n2, so we divide the numerator and the denominator by n2 and get

limn→∞9n2−4n−9n2=limn→∞(9n2n2−4n2)(nn2−9n2n2)=limn→∞(9−4n2)(1n−9)=9−00−9=−1.

Consequently, the sequence converges and its limit is −1.

question.name: Question 5
question.worked_solution:
To determine whether the sequence converges or diverges, we need to determine the limit of the sequence as $n$ approaches infinity:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{12n+1}{3n}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $3n,$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by $n$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{12n+1}{3n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{12n}{n}+\frac{1}{n})}{\frac{3n}{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{12+\frac{1}{n}}{3} \\  & =\frac{12+0}{3} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sequence converges, and its limit is $4.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Solve the inequality $-5z\le -1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The variable $z$ is being *multiplied* by $-5.$ To isolate $z,$ we perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $-5.$ Remember to perform the same operation on both sides.

Also, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5z\,\, & \le \,\,-1 \\ \frac{-5z}{-5}\,\, & \ge \,\,\frac{-1}{-5} \\ \frac{-5z}{-5}\,\, & \ge \,\,\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $-5$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-5z}{-5} & \ge \frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{-5}z}{\cancel{-5}} & \ge \frac{1}{5} \\ z & \ge \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $z\ge \frac{1}{5}.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Solve the inequality $4\le x+7.$
questions.worked_solution:
To isolate $x,$ we need to perform the *opposite* of *adding* $7,$ which is *subtracting* $7.$ Remember to perform the same operation on both sides.

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & \le x+7 \\ 4-7 & \le x+7-7 \\ -3 & \le x+0 \\ -3 & \le x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the inequality with the variable on the left-hand side:

$$
x\ge -3
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -3.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Solve the inequality $-\frac{x}{2}\le 4.$
questions.worked_solution:
The variable $x$ is being *divided* by $2.$ To isolate $x$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-2.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{x}{2}\,\, & \le \,\,4 \\ (-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2})\,\, & \ge \,\,(-2)\cdot 4 \\ (-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2})\,\, & \ge \,\,-8\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ (\cancel{-}2)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ 2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $2$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & \ge -8 \\ x & \ge -8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -8.$

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{x}{2}\,\, & \le \,\,4 \\ (-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2})\,\, & \ge \,\,(-2)\cdot 4 \\ (-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2})\,\, & \ge \,\,-8\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ (\cancel{-}2)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ 2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $2$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & \ge -8 \\ x & \ge -8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -8.$

−x2≤4(−2)⋅(−x2)≥(−2)⋅4(−2)⋅(−x2)≥−8

(−2)⋅(−x2)≥−8(−2)⋅(−x2)≥−82⋅x2≥−8

question.problem: Solve the inequality $-5z\le -1.$
question.worked_solution:
The variable $z$ is being *multiplied* by $-5.$ To isolate $z,$ we perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $-5.$ Remember to perform the same operation on both sides.

Also, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5z\,\, & \le \,\,-1 \\ \frac{-5z}{-5}\,\, & \ge \,\,\frac{-1}{-5} \\ \frac{-5z}{-5}\,\, & \ge \,\,\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $-5$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-5z}{-5} & \ge \frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{-5}z}{\cancel{-5}} & \ge \frac{1}{5} \\ z & \ge \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $z\ge \frac{1}{5}.$

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Solve the inequality $-5z\le -1.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The variable $z$ is being *multiplied* by $-5.$ To isolate $z,$ we perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $-5.$ Remember to perform the same operation on both sides.

Also, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5z\,\, & \le \,\,-1 \\ \frac{-5z}{-5}\,\, & \ge \,\,\frac{-1}{-5} \\ \frac{-5z}{-5}\,\, & \ge \,\,\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $-5$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-5z}{-5} & \ge \frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{-5}z}{\cancel{-5}} & \ge \frac{1}{5} \\ z & \ge \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $z\ge \frac{1}{5}.$

question.problem: Solve the inequality $4\le x+7.$
question.worked_solution:
To isolate $x,$ we need to perform the *opposite* of *adding* $7,$ which is *subtracting* $7.$ Remember to perform the same operation on both sides.

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & \le x+7 \\ 4-7 & \le x+7-7 \\ -3 & \le x+0 \\ -3 & \le x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the inequality with the variable on the left-hand side:

$$
x\ge -3
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -3.$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Solve the inequality $-\frac{x}{2}\le 4.$
question.worked_solution:
The variable $x$ is being *divided* by $2.$ To isolate $x$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-2.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{x}{2}\,\, & \le \,\,4 \\ (-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2})\,\, & \ge \,\,(-2)\cdot 4 \\ (-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2})\,\, & \ge \,\,-8\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)\cdot (-\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ (\cancel{-}2)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{x}{2}) & \ge -8 \\ 2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $2$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot \frac{x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & \ge -8 \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & \ge -8 \\ x & \ge -8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -8.$

$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨4y,\,5x,\,2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=3$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 3.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=3$ for  $1\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 3,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨4y,\,5x,\,2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4y,\,5x,\,6⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}6\,\text{d}S \\  & =6{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{3}\text{d}y{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot (3-1)\cdot (2-1) \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨yz,\,xz,\,xy⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=4$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=4$ for  $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=4$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨yz,\,xz,\,xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4y,\,4x,\,xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}xy\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{-1}^{1}\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =0\cdot 2 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨1-{e}^{z},\,xy,\,-3⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨3,\,1,\,1⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨1-{e}^{z},\,xy,\,-3⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨3,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨1-{e}^{z},\,xy,\,-3⟩\cdot ⟨3,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(3(1-{e}^{z})+xy-3) \\  & =\frac{xy-3{e}^{z}}{\sqrt{11}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{xy-3{e}^{z}}{\sqrt{11}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}{∬}_{S}xy-3{e}^{z}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{5}⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{5}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\cdot ⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2z+0-3(z-y)) \\  & =\frac{3y-z}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{3y-z}{5}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{∬}_{S}3y-z\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x-y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{6}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,6-y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+3)+(x+y)+(6-y)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{6} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane
questions.raw_html:
5.Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane?

Consider the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨x+3,x+y,z−x+6⟩ and a finite region S of the plane z=x−y such that Area(S)=6. Calculate the flux of F through S with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector n.

E
Wed, Oct 14th @ 8:43 PM|Elapsed: 0:12Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=3$ for  $1\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 3,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨4y,\,5x,\,2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4y,\,5x,\,6⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}6\,\text{d}S \\  & =6{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{3}\text{d}y{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot (3-1)\cdot (2-1) \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Consider the vector field F and the surface S with unit normal vector n, where

F(x,y,z)=⟨1−ez,xy,−3⟩,n(x,y,z)=111⟨3,1,1⟩.

If the flux of F across S with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=111∬SAAAAAAAdS,

what is the missing expression?

a
xy−3ez
b
xy−3−ez
c
xy+ez
d
xy+6
e
3ez+xy+3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If S is an oriented surface with unit normal vector n, and F is continuous vector field, then the flux of F across S measured with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS.

Calculating the dot product, we have

F⋅n=⟨1−ez,xy,−3⟩⋅111⟨3,1,1⟩=111⟨1−ez,xy,−3⟩⋅⟨3,1,1⟩=111(3(1−ez)+xy−3)=xy−3ez11.

Therefore, the flux can be written as

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬Sxy−3ez11dS=111∬Sxy−3ezdS.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\cdot ⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2z+0-3(z-y)) \\  & =\frac{3y-z}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{3y-z}{5}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{∬}_{S}3y-z\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,6-y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+3)+(x+y)+(6-y)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{6} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨x+3,x+y,z−x+6⟩ and a finite region S of the plane z=x−y such that Area(S)=6. Calculate the flux of F through S with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector n.

a
23
b
6
c
3
d
3
e
32
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If S is an oriented surface with unit normal vector n, and F is continuous vector field, then the flux of F across S measured with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS.

Notice that our surface z=x−y can be written using the dot product as

⟨x,y,z⟩⋅⟨−1,1,1⟩⏟n~=0,or⟨x,y,z⟩⋅⟨1,−1,−1⟩⏟−n~=0.

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface S, we must select one where the z-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

n~=⟨−1,1,1⟩.

Normalizing this vector, we get

n=n~‖n~‖=⟨−1,1,1⟩(−1)2+12+12=13⟨−1,1,1⟩.

Using the fact that z=x−y on S, we have

F⋅n=⟨x+3,x+y,z−x+6⟩⋅13⟨−1,1,1⟩=13⟨x+3,x+y,6−y⟩⋅⟨−1,1,1⟩=13(−(x+3)+(x+y)+(6−y))=33=3.

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of F across S as follows:

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬S3dS=3∬SdS=3⋅Area(S)=3⋅6=32.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨4y,\,5x,\,2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=3$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 3.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
question.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=3$ for  $1\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 3,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨4y,\,5x,\,2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4y,\,5x,\,6⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}6\,\text{d}S \\  & =6{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{3}\text{d}y{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot (3-1)\cdot (2-1) \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨4y,5x,2z⟩ and the surface S defined in Cartesian coordinates as z=3 for 1≤x≤2 and 1≤y≤3. Calculate the flux of F through S with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector n.

a
3
b
4
c
18
d
 12
e
 6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If S is an oriented surface with unit normal vector n, and F is continuous vector field, then the flux of F across S measured with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS.

For the surface z=3 for 1≤x≤2 and 1≤y≤3, the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

n=⟨0,0,1⟩.

Using the fact that z=3 on S, we have

F⋅n=⟨4y,5x,2z⟩⋅⟨0,0,1⟩=⟨4y,5x,6⟩⋅⟨0,0,1⟩=6.

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of F across S as follows:

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬S6dS=6∬DdA=6∫13∫12dxdy=6∫13dy∫12dx=6⋅(3−1)⋅(2−1)=12

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨yz,\,xz,\,xy⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=4$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
question.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=4$ for  $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=4$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨yz,\,xz,\,xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4y,\,4x,\,xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}xy\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{-1}^{1}\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =0\cdot 2 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨1-{e}^{z},\,xy,\,-3⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨3,\,1,\,1⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
question.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨1-{e}^{z},\,xy,\,-3⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨3,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨1-{e}^{z},\,xy,\,-3⟩\cdot ⟨3,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(3(1-{e}^{z})+xy-3) \\  & =\frac{xy-3{e}^{z}}{\sqrt{11}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{xy-3{e}^{z}}{\sqrt{11}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}{∬}_{S}xy-3{e}^{z}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the vector field F and the surface S with unit normal vector n, where

F(x,y,z)=⟨1−ez,xy,−3⟩,n(x,y,z)=111⟨3,1,1⟩.

If the flux of F across S with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=111∬SAAAAAAAdS,

what is the missing expression?

a
xy−3ez
b
xy−3−ez
c
xy+ez
d
xy+6
e
3ez+xy+3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If S is an oriented surface with unit normal vector n, and F is continuous vector field, then the flux of F across S measured with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS.

Calculating the dot product, we have

F⋅n=⟨1−ez,xy,−3⟩⋅111⟨3,1,1⟩=111⟨1−ez,xy,−3⟩⋅⟨3,1,1⟩=111(3(1−ez)+xy−3)=xy−3ez11.

Therefore, the flux can be written as

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬Sxy−3ez11dS=111∬Sxy−3ezdS.

Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{5}⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{5}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
question.worked_solution:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\cdot ⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2z+0-3(z-y)) \\  & =\frac{3y-z}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{3y-z}{5}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{∬}_{S}3y-z\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the vector field F and the surface S with unit normal vector n, where

F(x,y,z)=⟨z2,x,z−y⟩,n(x,y,z)=15⟨4,0,−3⟩.

If the flux of F across S with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=15∬SAAAAAAAdS,

what is the missing expression?

a
y−z
b
3y−z
c
y+4z
d
x+2y−z
e
x+3y+z2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If S is an oriented surface with unit normal vector n, and F is continuous vector field, then the flux of F across S measured with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS.

Calculating the dot product, we have

F⋅n=⟨z2,x,z−y⟩⋅15⟨4,0,−3⟩=15⟨z2,x,z−y⟩⋅⟨4,0,−3⟩=15(2z+0−3(z−y))=3y−z5.

Therefore, the flux can be written as

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬S3y−z5dS=15∬S3y−zdS.

last_observation.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\cdot ⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2z+0-3(z-y)) \\  & =\frac{3y-z}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{3y-z}{5}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{∬}_{S}3y-z\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the vector field F and the surface S with unit normal vector n, where

F(x,y,z)=⟨z2,x,z−y⟩,n(x,y,z)=15⟨4,0,−3⟩.

If the flux of F across S with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=15∬SAAAAAAAdS,

what is the missing expression?

a
y−z
b
3y−z
c
y+4z
d
x+2y−z
e
x+3y+z2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If S is an oriented surface with unit normal vector n, and F is continuous vector field, then the flux of F across S measured with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS.

Calculating the dot product, we have

F⋅n=⟨z2,x,z−y⟩⋅15⟨4,0,−3⟩=15⟨z2,x,z−y⟩⋅⟨4,0,−3⟩=15(2z+0−3(z−y))=3y−z5.

Therefore, the flux can be written as

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬S3y−z5dS=15∬S3y−zdS.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x-y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{6}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
question.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,6-y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+3)+(x+y)+(6-y)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{6} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨x+3,x+y,z−x+6⟩ and a finite region S of the plane z=x−y such that Area(S)=6. Calculate the flux of F through S with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector n.

a
23
b
6
c
3
d
3
e
32
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If S is an oriented surface with unit normal vector n, and F is continuous vector field, then the flux of F across S measured with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS.

Notice that our surface z=x−y can be written using the dot product as

⟨x,y,z⟩⋅⟨−1,1,1⟩⏟n~=0,or⟨x,y,z⟩⋅⟨1,−1,−1⟩⏟−n~=0.

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface S, we must select one where the z-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

n~=⟨−1,1,1⟩.

Normalizing this vector, we get

n=n~‖n~‖=⟨−1,1,1⟩(−1)2+12+12=13⟨−1,1,1⟩.

Using the fact that z=x−y on S, we have

F⋅n=⟨x+3,x+y,z−x+6⟩⋅13⟨−1,1,1⟩=13⟨x+3,x+y,6−y⟩⋅⟨−1,1,1⟩=13(−(x+3)+(x+y)+(6−y))=33=3.

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of F across S as follows:

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬S3dS=3∬SdS=3⋅Area(S)=3⋅6=32.

question.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨x+3,x+y,z−x+6⟩ and a finite region S of the plane z=x−y such that Area(S)=6. Calculate the flux of F through S with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector n.

a
23
b
6
c
3
d
3
e
32
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If S is an oriented surface with unit normal vector n, and F is continuous vector field, then the flux of F across S measured with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS.

Notice that our surface z=x−y can be written using the dot product as

⟨x,y,z⟩⋅⟨−1,1,1⟩⏟n~=0,or⟨x,y,z⟩⋅⟨1,−1,−1⟩⏟−n~=0.

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface S, we must select one where the z-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

n~=⟨−1,1,1⟩.

Normalizing this vector, we get

n=n~‖n~‖=⟨−1,1,1⟩(−1)2+12+12=13⟨−1,1,1⟩.

Using the fact that z=x−y on S, we have

F⋅n=⟨x+3,x+y,z−x+6⟩⋅13⟨−1,1,1⟩=13⟨x+3,x+y,6−y⟩⋅⟨−1,1,1⟩=13(−(x+3)+(x+y)+(6−y))=33=3.

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of F across S as follows:

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬S3dS=3∬SdS=3⋅Area(S)=3⋅6=32.

solution.reasoning: The upward unit normal is \langle-1,1,1\rangle/\sqrt{3}. Thus F\cdot n=(y+z-x+3)/\sqrt{3}=\sqrt{3} on z=x-y. The flux is \sqrt{3}\,\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{3}\sqrt{6}=3\sqrt{2}, option e. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x-y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{6}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,6-y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+3)+(x+y)+(6-y)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{6} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/9389d3d0d9206b72f379a328819e4624da3a294fc3222f048edc53957a8679ac.png)

Identify the differential equation that generated the slope field above.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/310d05d05284201c4914de171e6ee6a7574784da4c9bf7d4e442cdf2a210722d.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slope lines on the same vertical line are all the same. This means that the slope does not vary with $y.$ In other words, ${y}^{′}$ is a function of $x$ only.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\  & {y}^{′}={e}^{x} \\  & {y}^{′}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the slopes become vertical as $x\to 0.$ 

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Notice that

$$
|{y}^{′}|=|\frac{1}{x}|\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to 0.
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x}$ become vertical as $x\to 0.$
By contrast, 

$$
{y}^{′}={e}^{x}\to 1\,\text{as}\,x\to 0,
$$

and

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}\to 0\,\text{as}\,x\to 0.
$$

Therefore, the required equation is

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/b45ab87c3b5f6b083ca5828676ca96486e3825b3b3fbbfc3f31d19fa65a215b5.png)

The diagram shown above is the slope field for which of the following differential equations?
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/ef837c5bdd4198651302e77b70d592c7771071a1ee3543ce76a3685b0439fa82.png)

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $x=-1$ and $y=-2,$ as shown above. Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should evaluate to zero on both of these lines. 

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(x+1)(y+2) \\ {y}^{′} & =(x+1)^{2}(y+2)\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the lines $x=-1$ and $y=-2$ divide the plane into $4$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $4$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| $y>-2$ | $↘$

$(-)$ | $↗$

$(+)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y<-2$ | $↗$

$(+)$ | $↘$

$(-)$ |
|  | $x<-1$ | $x>-1$ |

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=(x+1)(y+2).
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/32165a622d57d6af278b7ce288093ef4db6867619046b8625071f0274a1c7e93.png)

Which of the following equations could have generated the slope field shown above?

I. ${y}^{′}={x}^{3}y+{x}^{3}$

II. ${y}^{′}=xy-x$

III. ${y}^{′}={x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/a278676af009b7096bd50f9b3918f0e8090c1822a9e029ac2b4b6325d1ba7a4c.png)

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $x=0$ and $y=-1,$ as shown above. Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should evaluate to zero on both of these lines.

- Second, the lines $x=0$ and $y=-1$ divide the plane into $4$ quarters. The sign of the slopes in each of the $4$ quarters are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| $y>-1$ | $↘$

$(-)$ | $↗$

$(+)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y<-1$ | $↗$

$(+)$ | $↘$

$(-)$ |
|  | $x<0$ | $x>0$ |

With that in mind, let's consider each equation.

- Equation I gives the required behavior. The right-hand side of 

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{3}y+{x}^{3}={x}^{3}(y+1)
$$

 evaluates to zero at $x=0$ and $y=-1,$ and the sign of the slopes in the required regions (summarized below) correspond to the given slope field.

| $y>-1$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y<-1$ | $+$ | $-$ |
|  | $x<0$ | $x>0$ |

- Equation II does *not* give the required behavior. The right-hand side of 

$$
{y}^{′}=xy-x=x(y-1)
$$

 evaluates to zero at $x=0$ and $y=1.$

- Equation III does *not* give the required behavior. The right-hand side of 

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}={x}^{2}(y+1)
$$

 evaluates to zero at $x=0$ and $y=-1,$ but the sign of the slopes in the required regions (summarized below) do not correspond to the given slope field.

| $y>-1$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y<-1$ | $-$ | $-$ |
|  | $x<0$ | $x>0$ |

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/84597fa3c8e0a187df5792e8a8289033e6549599b1df5a34073049a5b3322770.png)

The diagram shown above is the slope field for which of the following differential equations?
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/3673d384035d7febd8540e34143c2a490f7aa3968752785ef809cff16d2524ce.png)

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $x=0$ and $x=2,$ as shown above. Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should evaluate to zero on both of these lines. 

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{2}-2x=x(x-2) \\ {y}^{′} & =2{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}={x}^{2}(2-x)\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the lines $x=0$ and $x=2$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| $x<0$ | $0<x<2$ | $x<2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $↗$

$(+)$ | $↘$

$(-)$ | $↗$

$(+)$ |

 
Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}-2x=x(x-2).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}={x}^{2}-2x.$

questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/a71217d2b2e610b38f78f4471cc122de7098708900e3658cda449118df0e63dd.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $x=0$ and $y=-1,$ as shown above. Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should evaluate to zero on both of these lines.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}={x}^{2}(y+1)^{2} \\ {y}^{′} & =x(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the lines $x=0$ and $y=-1$ divide the plane into $4$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $4$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| $y>-1$ | $↗$

$(+)$ | $↗$

$(+)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y<-1$ | $↗$

$(+)$ | $↗$

$(+)$ |
|  | $x<0$ | $x>0$ |

 
Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}={x}^{2}(y+1)^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}.$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/310d05d05284201c4914de171e6ee6a7574784da4c9bf7d4e442cdf2a210722d.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slope lines on the same vertical line are all the same. This means that the slope does not vary with $y.$ In other words, ${y}^{′}$ is a function of $x$ only.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\  & {y}^{′}={e}^{x} \\  & {y}^{′}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the slopes become vertical as $x\to 0.$ 

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Notice that

$$
|{y}^{′}|=|\frac{1}{x}|\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to 0.
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x}$ become vertical as $x\to 0.$
By contrast, 

$$
{y}^{′}={e}^{x}\to 1\,\text{as}\,x\to 0,
$$

and

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}\to 0\,\text{as}\,x\to 0.
$$

Therefore, the required equation is

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Identify the differential equation that generated the slope field above.
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/310d05d05284201c4914de171e6ee6a7574784da4c9bf7d4e442cdf2a210722d.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slope lines on the same vertical line are all the same. This means that the slope does not vary with $y.$ In other words, ${y}^{′}$ is a function of $x$ only.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\  & {y}^{′}={e}^{x} \\  & {y}^{′}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the slopes become vertical as $x\to 0.$ 

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Notice that

$$
|{y}^{′}|=|\frac{1}{x}|\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to 0.
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x}$ become vertical as $x\to 0.$
By contrast, 

$$
{y}^{′}={e}^{x}\to 1\,\text{as}\,x\to 0,
$$

and

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}\to 0\,\text{as}\,x\to 0.
$$

Therefore, the required equation is

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Question 1
?

Identify the differential equation that generated the slope field above.

a
y′=ex
b
y′=1x+1y
c
y′=1x
d
y′=1y
e
y′=x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

  • First, the slope lines on the same vertical line are all the same. This means that the slope does not vary with y. In other words, y′ is a function of x only.

    Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following: y′=1xy′=exy′=x2

  • Second, the slopes become vertical as x→0.

    Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is y′=1x. Notice that |y′|=|1x|→∞asx→0. Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for the differential equation y′=1x become vertical as x→0. By contrast, y′=ex→1asx→0, and y′=x2→0asx→0.

Therefore, the required equation is y′=1x.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223512/assets/ef837c5bdd4198651302e77b70d592c7771071a1ee3543ce76a3685b0439fa82.png)

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $x=-1$ and $y=-2,$ as shown above. Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should evaluate to zero on both of these lines. 

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(x+1)(y+2) \\ {y}^{′} & =(x+1)^{2}(y+2)\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the lines $x=-1$ and $y=-2$ divide the plane into $4$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $4$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| $y>-2$ | $↘$

$(-)$ | $↗$

$(+)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y<-2$ | $↗$

$(+)$ | $↘$

$(-)$ |
|  | $x<-1$ | $x>-1$ |

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=(x+1)(y+2).
$$
