question.html:
Question 9
?

What is ∫252x1/3dx expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+3jn)1/3⋅3n]
b
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+3jn)⋅3n]
c
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(3jn)1/3⋅3n]
d
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[(3+3jn)1/3⋅3n]
e
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+2jn)1/3⋅2n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1f(xj)⋅Δx,

where Δx=b−an and xj=a+jΔx.

In the definite integral

∫252x1/3dx,

the function is f(x)=2x1/3, the lower bound is a=2, and the upper bound is b=5. So, we have

Δx=5−2n=3n,

and therefore

∫252x1/3dx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1f(xj)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[f(2+j⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[f(2+3jn)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+3jn)1/3⋅3n].
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum

solution.reasoning: The width is Δx=(5-2)/n=3/n, and the left endpoints are x_j=2+3j/n for j=0,...,n-1. Substituting into 2x^{1/3} gives option a. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem: What is ${\int }_{2}^{5}2{x}^{1/3}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
feedback.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{2}^{5}2{x}^{1/3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=2{x}^{1/3},$ the lower bound is $a=2,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-2}{n}=\frac{3}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{5}2{x}^{1/3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[f(2+j\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[f(2+\frac{3j}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[2{(2+\frac{3j}{n})}^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

What is ∫252x1/3dx expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+3jn)1/3⋅3n]
b
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+3jn)⋅3n]
c
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(3jn)1/3⋅3n]
d
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[(3+3jn)1/3⋅3n]
e
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+2jn)1/3⋅2n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1f(xj)⋅Δx,

where Δx=b−an and xj=a+jΔx.

In the definite integral

∫252x1/3dx,

the function is f(x)=2x1/3, the lower bound is a=2, and the upper bound is b=5. So, we have

Δx=5−2n=3n,

and therefore

∫252x1/3dx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1f(xj)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[f(2+j⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[f(2+3jn)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+3jn)1/3⋅3n].

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: What is ${\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
question.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{l})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{l}=a+lΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{2},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{n}=\frac{1}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{l})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[f(1+l\cdot \frac{1}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{l}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{l}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 10
?

What is ∫12x2dx expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?

a
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+2ln)2⋅1n]
b
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(2+ln)2⋅1n]
c
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+ln)2⋅1n]
d
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+2ln)2⋅2n]
e
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[−(2+ln)2⋅2n]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1f(xl)⋅Δx,

where Δx=b−an and xl=a+lΔx.

In the definite integral

∫12x2dx,

the function is f(x)=x2, the lower bound is a=1, and the upper bound is b=2. So, we have Δx=2−1n=1n,

and therefore

∫12x2dx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1f(xl)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[f(1+l⋅1n)⋅1n]=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[f(1+ln)⋅1n]=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+ln)2⋅1n].

last_observation.name: Question 10
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum
last_observation.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{l})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{l}=a+lΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{2},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{n}=\frac{1}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{l})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[f(1+l\cdot \frac{1}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{l}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{l}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 10
?

What is ∫12x2dx expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?

a
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+2ln)2⋅1n]
b
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(2+ln)2⋅1n]
c
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+ln)2⋅1n]
d
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+2ln)2⋅2n]
e
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[−(2+ln)2⋅2n]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1f(xl)⋅Δx,

where Δx=b−an and xl=a+lΔx.

In the definite integral

∫12x2dx,

the function is f(x)=x2, the lower bound is a=1, and the upper bound is b=2. So, we have Δx=2−1n=1n,

and therefore

∫12x2dx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1f(xl)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[f(1+l⋅1n)⋅1n]=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[f(1+ln)⋅1n]=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+ln)2⋅1n].
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum

solution.reasoning: The width is Δx=(2-1)/n=1/n, and the left endpoints are x_l=1+l/n for l=0,...,n-1. Substituting into x^2 gives option c. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 10
feedback.problem: What is ${\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
feedback.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{l})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{l}=a+lΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{2},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{n}=\frac{1}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{l})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[f(1+l\cdot \frac{1}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{l}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{l}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

What is ∫12x2dx expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?

a
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+2ln)2⋅1n]
b
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(2+ln)2⋅1n]
c
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+ln)2⋅1n]
d
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+2ln)2⋅2n]
e
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[−(2+ln)2⋅2n]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1f(xl)⋅Δx,

where Δx=b−an and xl=a+lΔx.

In the definite integral

∫12x2dx,

the function is f(x)=x2, the lower bound is a=1, and the upper bound is b=2. So, we have Δx=2−1n=1n,

and therefore

∫12x2dx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1f(xl)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[f(1+l⋅1n)⋅1n]=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[f(1+ln)⋅1n]=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+ln)2⋅1n].

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that

$$
{\int }_{2}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[5{(2+\frac{4k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

$\,f(x)=$
{{field-1}} $\,$ and 
$\,b=$
{{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=2.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{4}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{4}{n}=\frac{b-2}{n}\,⟹\,b=6.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=2+\frac{4k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=5{x}_{k}^{3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{2}^{6}5{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[5{(2+\frac{4k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$
f(x)=5{x}^{3}\,\text{and}\,b=6.
$$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{2}(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{((-1+\frac{3k}{n})+8)}^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$

question.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=-1.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{3}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{3}{n}=\frac{b-(-1)}{n}\,⟹\,b=2.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=-1+\frac{3k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=({x}_{k}+8)^{1/3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{2}(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{((-1+\frac{3k}{n})+8)}^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].
$$

$$
f(x)=(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{and}\,b=2.

question.name: Question 13
question.problem: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{e}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{ie}{n})\cdot \frac{e}{n}].$
question.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=e.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{e}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{e}{n}=\frac{b-e}{n}\,⟹\,b=2e.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{i}=e+\frac{ie}{n}$ and $f({x}_{i})=\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{e}^{2e}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{ie}{n})\cdot \frac{e}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and $b=2e.$

last_observation.name: Question 13
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum as a Definite Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=e.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{e}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{e}{n}=\frac{b-e}{n}\,⟹\,b=2e.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{i}=e+\frac{ie}{n}$ and $f({x}_{i})=\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{e}^{2e}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{ie}{n})\cdot \frac{e}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and $b=2e.$

question.html:
Question 13
?

Find the function f(x) and the value of b, given that ∫ebf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[ln⁡(e+ien)⋅en].

a
f(x)=ln⁡x and b=2e
b
f(x)=ln⁡(x+e) and b=e+1
c
f(x)=ln⁡(x+e) and b=2e
d
f(x)=ln⁡(x+e) and b=e2
e
f(x)=ln⁡x and b=e2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows: ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1f(xi)⋅Δx where Δx=b−an and xi=a+iΔx.

Notice that we're given that the lower limit a=e.

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that Δx=en. Therefore, en=b−en⟹b=2e.

Consequently, xi=e+ien and f(xi)=ln⁡xi.

Hence, ∫e2eln⁡xdx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[ln⁡(e+ien)⋅en].

Therefore, the correct answer is f(x)=ln⁡x and b=2e.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum as a Definite Integral

solution.reasoning: The width is Δx=e/n and the left endpoints are x_i=e+ie/n. Thus f(x)=ln(x) and b-e=e, giving b=2e and option a. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.problem: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{e}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{ie}{n})\cdot \frac{e}{n}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=e.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{e}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{e}{n}=\frac{b-e}{n}\,⟹\,b=2e.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{i}=e+\frac{ie}{n}$ and $f({x}_{i})=\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{e}^{2e}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{ie}{n})\cdot \frac{e}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and $b=2e.$

Question 13
?

Find the function f(x) and the value of b, given that ∫ebf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[ln⁡(e+ien)⋅en].

a
f(x)=ln⁡x and b=2e
b
f(x)=ln⁡(x+e) and b=e+1
c
f(x)=ln⁡(x+e) and b=2e
d
f(x)=ln⁡(x+e) and b=e2
e
f(x)=ln⁡x and b=e2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows: ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1f(xi)⋅Δx where Δx=b−an and xi=a+iΔx.

Notice that we're given that the lower limit a=e.

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that Δx=en. Therefore, en=b−en⟹b=2e.

Consequently, xi=e+ien and f(xi)=ln⁡xi.

Hence, ∫e2eln⁡xdx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[ln⁡(e+ien)⋅en].

Therefore, the correct answer is f(x)=ln⁡x and b=2e.

question.name: Question 14
question.problem: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{0}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{6i/n}\cdot \frac{6}{n}].$
question.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=0.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{6}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{6}{n}=\frac{b-0}{n}\,⟹\,b=6.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{i}=\frac{6i}{n}$ and $f({x}_{i})={e}^{{x}_{i}}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{6i/n}\cdot \frac{6}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)={e}^{x}$ and $b=6.$

last_observation.name: Question 14
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum as a Definite Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=0.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{6}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{6}{n}=\frac{b-0}{n}\,⟹\,b=6.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{i}=\frac{6i}{n}$ and $f({x}_{i})={e}^{{x}_{i}}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{6i/n}\cdot \frac{6}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)={e}^{x}$ and $b=6.$

question.html:
Question 14
?

Find the function f(x) and the value of b, given that ∫0bf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[e6i/n⋅6n].

a
f(x)=e6x and b=6
b
f(x)=e6x and b=1
c
f(x)=ex and b=1
d
f(x)=ex and b=6
e
f(x)=e2x and b=3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows: ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1f(xi)⋅Δx where Δx=b−an and xi=a+iΔx.

Notice that we're given that the lower limit a=0.

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that Δx=6n. Therefore, 6n=b−0n⟹b=6.

Consequently, xi=6in and f(xi)=exi.

Hence, ∫06exdx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[e6i/n⋅6n].

Therefore, the correct answer is f(x)=ex and b=6.

feedback.name: Question 14
feedback.problem: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{0}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{6i/n}\cdot \frac{6}{n}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=0.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{6}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{6}{n}=\frac{b-0}{n}\,⟹\,b=6.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{i}=\frac{6i}{n}$ and $f({x}_{i})={e}^{{x}_{i}}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{6i/n}\cdot \frac{6}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)={e}^{x}$ and $b=6.$

question.problem:
Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that

$$
{\int }_{1}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{\,1+4k/n}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

$\,f(x)=$

question.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=1.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{4}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{4}{n}=\frac{b-1}{n}\,⟹\,b=5.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=1+\frac{4k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})={e}^{\,{x}_{k}}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{\,1+4k/n}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$
f(x)={e}^{x}\,\text{and}\,b=5.
$$

question.name: Question 16
question.problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
question.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(0+k\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 16
?

What is ∫03arctan⁡xdx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(kn)⋅1n]
b
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅1n]
c
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅3n]
d
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(k3n)⋅3n]
e
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅13n]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx, where xk=a+kΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral ∫03arctan⁡xdx, the function is f(x)=arctan⁡x, the lower bound is a=0 and the upper bound is b=3. So, we have Δx=3−0n=3n.

Therefore, ∫03arctan⁡xdx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(0+k⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(3kn)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅3n].

last_observation.name: Question 16
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Right Riemann Sum
last_observation.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(0+k\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 16
?

What is ∫03arctan⁡xdx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(kn)⋅1n]
b
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅1n]
c
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅3n]
d
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(k3n)⋅3n]
e
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅13n]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx, where xk=a+kΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral ∫03arctan⁡xdx, the function is f(x)=arctan⁡x, the lower bound is a=0 and the upper bound is b=3. So, we have Δx=3−0n=3n.

Therefore, ∫03arctan⁡xdx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(0+k⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(3kn)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅3n].
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Right Riemann Sum

solution.reasoning: The width is Δx=(3-0)/n=3/n, and the right endpoints are x_k=3k/n for k=1,...,n. Substituting into arctan(x) gives option c. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 16
feedback.problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
feedback.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(0+k\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16
?

What is ∫03arctan⁡xdx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(kn)⋅1n]
b
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅1n]
c
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅3n]
d
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(k3n)⋅3n]
e
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅13n]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx, where xk=a+kΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral ∫03arctan⁡xdx, the function is f(x)=arctan⁡x, the lower bound is a=0 and the upper bound is b=3. So, we have Δx=3−0n=3n.

Therefore, ∫03arctan⁡xdx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(0+k⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(3kn)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅3n].

question.name: Question 17
question.problem: What is ${\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
question.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=-2{x}^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=-2$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-(-2)}{n}=\frac{5}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+k\cdot \frac{5}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+\frac{5k}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[-2{(-2+\frac{5k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{5}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 17
?

What is ∫−23−2x3dx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(2+kn)3⋅1n]
b
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(5+2kn)⋅2n]
c
limn→∞∑k=1n[−(−1+5kn)3⋅5n]
d
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(5kn)−2⋅5n]
e
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(−2+5kn)3⋅5n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx,

where xk=a+kΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral

∫−23−2x3dx,

the function is f(x)=−2x3, the lower bound is a=−2 and the upper bound is b=3. So, we have

Δx=3−(−2)n=5n.

Therefore,

∫−23−2x3dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(−2+k⋅5n)⋅5n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(−2+5kn)⋅5n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(−2+5kn)3⋅5n].

last_observation.name: Question 17
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Right Riemann Sum
last_observation.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=-2{x}^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=-2$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-(-2)}{n}=\frac{5}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+k\cdot \frac{5}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+\frac{5k}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[-2{(-2+\frac{5k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{5}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 17
?

What is ∫−23−2x3dx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(2+kn)3⋅1n]
b
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(5+2kn)⋅2n]
c
limn→∞∑k=1n[−(−1+5kn)3⋅5n]
d
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(5kn)−2⋅5n]
e
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(−2+5kn)3⋅5n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx,

where xk=a+kΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral

∫−23−2x3dx,

the function is f(x)=−2x3, the lower bound is a=−2 and the upper bound is b=3. So, we have

Δx=3−(−2)n=5n.

Therefore,

∫−23−2x3dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(−2+k⋅5n)⋅5n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(−2+5kn)⋅5n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(−2+5kn)3⋅5n].
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Right Riemann Sum

solution.reasoning: The width is Δx=(3-(-2))/n=5/n, and the right endpoints are x_k=-2+5k/n for k=1,...,n. Substituting into -2x^3 gives option e. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 17
feedback.problem: What is ${\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
feedback.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=-2{x}^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=-2$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-(-2)}{n}=\frac{5}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+k\cdot \frac{5}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+\frac{5k}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[-2{(-2+\frac{5k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{5}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 18
question.problem:
What is ${\int }_{1}^{4}(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{1}^{4}(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[($
{{field-1}}
$)^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}]$
question.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{4}(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=(x+8)^{1/3},$ the lower bound is $a=1$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{4-1}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(1+\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[{((1+\frac{3i}{n})+8)}^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[{(\,9+\frac{3i}{n}\,)}^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: What is ${\int }_{-4}^{-1}\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4}\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
question.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{-1}\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4},$ the lower bound is $a=-4$ and the upper bound is $b=-1.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{-1-(-4)}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{-1}\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(-4+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(-4+\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[\sqrt{5}{(-4+\frac{3i}{n})}^{-4}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

What is ∫−4−15x−4dx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−2+3in)−2⋅3n]
b
limn→∞∑i=1n[5−2+5in⋅5n]
c
limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−4+3in)−4⋅3n]
d
limn→∞∑i=1n[5−4+3in⋅3n]
e
limn→∞∑i=1n[(−4+2in)−4⋅2n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=1nf(xi)⋅Δx,

where xi=a+iΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral

∫−4−15x−4dx,

the function is f(x)=5x−4, the lower bound is a=−4 and the upper bound is b=−1. So, we have

Δx=−1−(−4)n=3n.

Therefore,

∫−4−15x−4dx=limn→∞∑i=1nf(xi)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑i=1n[f(−4+i⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑i=1n[f(−4+3in)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−4+3in)−4⋅3n].

last_observation.name: Question 19
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Right Riemann Sum
last_observation.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{-1}\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4},$ the lower bound is $a=-4$ and the upper bound is $b=-1.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{-1-(-4)}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{-1}\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(-4+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(-4+\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[\sqrt{5}{(-4+\frac{3i}{n})}^{-4}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 19
?

What is ∫−4−15x−4dx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−2+3in)−2⋅3n]
b
limn→∞∑i=1n[5−2+5in⋅5n]
c
limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−4+3in)−4⋅3n]
d
limn→∞∑i=1n[5−4+3in⋅3n]
e
limn→∞∑i=1n[(−4+2in)−4⋅2n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=1nf(xi)⋅Δx,

where xi=a+iΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral

∫−4−15x−4dx,

the function is f(x)=5x−4, the lower bound is a=−4 and the upper bound is b=−1. So, we have

Δx=−1−(−4)n=3n.

Therefore,

∫−4−15x−4dx=limn→∞∑i=1nf(xi)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑i=1n[f(−4+i⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑i=1n[f(−4+3in)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−4+3in)−4⋅3n].
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Right Riemann Sum

solution.reasoning: The width is Δx=(-1-(-4))/n=3/n, and the right endpoints are x_i=-4+3i/n for i=1,...,n. Substituting into sqrt(5)x^{-4} gives option c. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 19
feedback.problem: What is ${\int }_{-4}^{-1}\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4}\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
feedback.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{-1}\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4},$ the lower bound is $a=-4$ and the upper bound is $b=-1.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{-1-(-4)}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{-1}\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(-4+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(-4+\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[\sqrt{5}{(-4+\frac{3i}{n})}^{-4}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

What is ∫−4−15x−4dx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−2+3in)−2⋅3n]
b
limn→∞∑i=1n[5−2+5in⋅5n]
c
limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−4+3in)−4⋅3n]
d
limn→∞∑i=1n[5−4+3in⋅3n]
e
limn→∞∑i=1n[(−4+2in)−4⋅2n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=1nf(xi)⋅Δx,

where xi=a+iΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral

∫−4−15x−4dx,

the function is f(x)=5x−4, the lower bound is a=−4 and the upper bound is b=−1. So, we have

Δx=−1−(−4)n=3n.

Therefore,

∫−4−15x−4dx=limn→∞∑i=1nf(xi)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑i=1n[f(−4+i⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑i=1n[f(−4+3in)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−4+3in)−4⋅3n].

question.name: Question 20
question.problem:
What is ${\int }_{2}^{5}8{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{2}^{5}8{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[8($
{{field-1}}
$)^{\,4}\cdot \frac{3}{n}]$
question.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{2}^{5}8{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=8{x}^{4},$ the lower bound is $a=2$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-2}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{5}8{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(2+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(2+\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[8{(\,2+\frac{3i}{n}\,)}^{\,4}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If ${\int }_{C}z\,\text{d}x+x\,\text{d}y+y\,\text{d}z$ is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for some piecewise smooth curve $C,$ then $F(x,y,z)=$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y+R\,\text{d}z
$$

In our case, $P=z,Q=x,R=y.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(z\,i+x\,j+y\,k)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}z\,\text{d}x+x\,\text{d}y+y\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $F=z\,i+x\,j+y\,k.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Let $F(x,y,z)=yz\,i+xz\,j+xy\,k$ and let $C$ be a path in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y+R(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}yz\,\text{d}x+xz\,\text{d}y+xy\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Let $F(x,y)={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ and let $C$ be the path defined by $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t-1⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}x+{e}^{x}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Let $F(x,y)=4\,i-(2y-3x)\,j$ and let $C$ be the path defined by $r(t)=⟨t,\,3t-1⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}4\,\text{d}x-(2y-3x)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/103c586778cdd8181fdc8396a92472df0525fc8e1c77fde9a7c3f731dca6df07.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $OABO,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup \{-{C}_{2}\}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ is the same path as ${C}_{2}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/fec5c3e96eeed9fb01479c0127e2d530a628855a124d8ab1ef380c48c2f569f1.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $LMNL,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup \{-{C}_{2}\}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ is the same path as ${C}_{2}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/746a05b2345e50173ed898b741944ba435d17a44dfc075848be9d8fcd2f2ad90.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $PQRP,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C=\{-{C}_{1}\}\cup {C}_{2}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{1}$ is the same path as ${C}_{1}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/9fd222d255fd1a37f00cbe7c9abf6af0d0e3af92f9ac581591bb1062780e69fa.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $ABCA,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the **clockwise** direction?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C=\{-{C}_{1}\}\cup {C}_{2}\cup \{-{C}_{3}\},
$$

where $-{C}_{1}$ and $-{C}_{3}$ are the same paths as ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{3}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/3121d24ea2b9eac3d95c34202619800331d4719c786b8f5a1051350370a1bea2.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $TUVT,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the **clockwise** direction?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C=\{-{C}_{1}\}\cup {C}_{2}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{1}$ is the same path as ${C}_{1}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/c0a4f042748ddadd824bed4ee71bca9724d7ca7dcc376a0ccf7c1353d59ec4fc.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(-2,2)$ to the point $B(-1,2),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(-1,2)$ to the point $D(-1,0).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-\frac{7}{2},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x-y)\,i+(y-x)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the vertical line segment from $B$ to $D.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(d-b) \\  & =⟨-1,2⟩+t(⟨-1,0⟩-⟨-1,2⟩) \\  & =⟨-1,2-2t⟩ \\  & =-\,i+(2-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=-1$ and $y=2-2t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(x-y)\,i+(y-x)\,j \\  & =(-1-(2-2t))\,i+(2-2t-(-1))\,j \\  & =(-3+2t)\,i+(3-2t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-2t)j \\  & =-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =((-3+2t)\,i+(3-2t)\,j)\cdot (-2\,j) \\  & =(3-2t)\cdot (-2) \\  & =4t-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+{\int }_{0}^{1}(4t-6)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+[2{t}^{2}-6t]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+[2({1}^{2})-6(1)-0] \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}-4 \\  & =-\frac{15}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/0457cb819e6f39ef9c0978e356cff788e1cf5edbef9cbf844a054ab777b70eac.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,1),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of the line segment from the point $B(0,1)$ to the point $D(1,1).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-\frac{3}{2},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x-2y)\,i+(y-x)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$  It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨-2,0⟩+t(⟨0,1⟩-⟨-2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨-2+2t,t⟩ \\  & =(-2+2t)i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=-2+2t$ and $y=t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =(x-2y)\,i+(y-x)\,j \\  & =((-2+2t)-2t)\,i+(t-(-2+2t))\,j \\  & =-2\,i+(2-t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(-2\,i+(2-t)\,j)\cdot (2\,i+j) \\  & =-2-t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+(-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-2-t)\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2} \\  & ={[-2t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =[-2(1)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-0]-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/512905447203d1d3a96781d20d586f9c4cf5cc9392fab50607b6fc77e9b00121.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a section of the parabola $y={x}^{2}$ from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(2,4),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(2,4)$ to the point $B(0,4).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-2,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

${C}_{1}$ is the section of parabola $y={x}^{2}$ from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<2.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =x\,i+y\,j \\  & =t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})j \\  & =i+2t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j)\cdot (i+2t\,j) \\  & =t+2{t}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t-2 \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(t+2{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t-2 \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}-2 \\  & =[2+8]-2 \\  & =10-2 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/0e4a78829ce8d1135d46dda1db59c968c0306937d9c5a45b24fa41648a679ea4.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(2,0),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(1,1).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i+(x-y)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨2,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨2-t,t⟩ \\  & =(2-t)\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=2-t$ and $y=t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(x+y)\,i+(x-y)\,j \\  & =(2-t+t)\,i+(2-t-t)\,j \\  & =2\,i+(2-2t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(2\,i+(2-2t)\,j)\cdot (-i+j) \\  & =-2+(2-2t) \\  & =-2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2-(1-0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/87182d625f4e669a6b2791a17f3e12c34922043b8f3deefd6b2473e8fb529886.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(2,0),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a section of the parabola $y=4-{x}^{2}$ from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(0,4).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

Let ${C}_{2}$ be the section of parabola $y=4-{x}^{2}$ from $A$ to $B.$ Then,
 $-{C}_{2}$ will be the same path but travelled from $B$ to $A.$ The path $-{C}_{2}$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t)=t\,i+(4-{t}^{2})\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<2.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y=4-{t}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =x\,i=t\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2})j \\  & =i-2t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i)\cdot (i-2t\,j) \\  & =t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =2-{\int }_{0}^{2}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2-{\int }_{0}^{2}t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2-{[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2-[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}] \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Establishing the Connection With Line Integrals of Scalar Fields
canonical_examples.problem: Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (3x+2) \: \mathbf{i} - y^3 \: \mathbf{j}$ and let $C$ be a path in $\mathbb R^2.$ Write $\displaystyle \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}$ in the form $\displaystyle\int_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x +  Q(x,y)\,\textrm d y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = P(x,y) \: \mathbf{i} + Q(x,y) \: \mathbf{j}
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_C P(x,y) \: \text{d}x + Q(x,y) \: \text{d}y.
$$

In our case, $P = 3x+2$ and $Q = -y^3.$ Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}(3x+2)\,\text{d}x-{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Establishing the Connection With Line Integrals of Scalar Fields

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/38ab4af726729b5c9804f4aa13801d637e5e62eda085d6611174586827ef8c11.png)

Consider the integral $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $FGHF$ shown above, traversed in the **clockwise** direction. Express this integral as a sum of line integrals along $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C = \{-C_1\} \cup \{-C_2\} \cup C_3,
$$

where $-C_1$ and $-C_2$ are the same paths as $C_1$ and $C_2$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/001487e4a94988a24d15702a18692e9deb2495a7cc7ec5c9f71b98fea13e0ce8.png)

The path $C_1$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $O(0,0),$ and the path $C_2$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $B(1,1).$

Given that $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = -4,$ evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x, y) = (2x-3y) \,\mathbf{i} + (2y-5x)\,\mathbf {j}$ and $C = C_1\cup C_2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}
+
 \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path $C_2$ is the line segment from $O$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(c-b) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨t,t⟩ \\  & =t\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \lt t \lt 1.$ Along this segment, we have $x = t$ and $y = t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(2x-3y)\,i+(2y-5x)\,j \\  & =(2t-3t)\,i+(2t-5t)\,j \\  & =-t\,i-3t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(-t\,i-3t\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =-t\cdot 1+(-3t)\cdot 1 \\  & =-4t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+[-2{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-4+[-2+0] \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Line integrals of vector-valued functions share a fundamental connection with line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y.$

Consider a vector field $\mathbf F$ on $\mathbb R^2$ with components $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j
$$

Now suppose that $C$ is a smooth curve on $\mathbb R^2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].
$$

Then, we can write the line integral of $\mathbf F$ along $C$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)  \,\textrm d y
$$

An analogous result holds for vector fields on $\mathbb R^3.$ That is, 

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y,z)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d y + R(x,y,z) \,\textrm d z
$$

where $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$

tutorials.name: Reversing the Orientation of a Curve and Sums Over Unions of Paths
tutorials.problem:
Since there is a fundamental link between line integrals of vector-valued functions and line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y,$ it should be unsurprising that they share similar properties. We list two of them below:

- If $-C$ denotes the path obtained by reversing the orientation of $C,$ then

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

- If $C = C_1\cup C_2$ is the union of two paths $C_1$ and $C_2$, then

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r 
= 
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

The first property has an intuitive meaning if we think about it in terms of the work done by a force on a particle. To see this, consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the line segment $\overline{AB},$ shown below. Let $C$ be the path defined by traversing the line segment from $A$ to $B.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/4f69f80d98d301410908f7ec867a89bdc834c22a51f224d9b00b80ceca39ab87.png)

 

Let $W(C)$ be the work done in moving the particle along $C.$ Since our particle moves in the same direction as the vector field, we have

$$
W(C) = \int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r > 0.
$$

However, if we move the particle from $B$ to $A,$ we expect the line integral to be negative. This is because the particle is now moving against $\mathbf F.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/fe6b2e67d33a4993104406c88b1dc0dc897be33d034007ed581a75f741ddf620.png)

 

Therefore,

$$
W(-C) = \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r < 0.
$$

We can show that the work done in moving the particle along $-C$ is the same as the work done in moving it along $C$ but with the opposite sign. That is

$$
W(-C) = -W(C).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)  \,\textrm d y
$$

An analogous result holds for vector fields on $\mathbb R^3.$ That is, 

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y,z)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d y + R(x,y,z) \,\textrm d z
$$

where $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$
tutorial.content:
Line integrals of vector-valued functions share a fundamental connection with line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y.$

Consider a vector field $\mathbf F$ on $\mathbb R^2$ with components $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j
$$

Now suppose that $C$ is a smooth curve on $\mathbb R^2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].
$$

Then, we can write the line integral of $\mathbf F$ along $C$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)  \,\textrm d y
$$

An analogous result holds for vector fields on $\mathbb R^3.$ That is, 

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y,z)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d y + R(x,y,z) \,\textrm d z
$$

where $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Let F(x,y,z)=yzi+xzj+xyk and let C be a path in R3. Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr?

a
∫Cxdx+ydy+zdz
b
∫C(yz+xz)dxdy+xydz
c
∫C(yz+xy+xy)dxdydz
d
∫Cyzdx+xzdy+xydz
e
∫Cyzdx+(xz+xy)dydz
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a piecewise-smooth path C and a vector field F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)i+Q(x,y,z)j+R(x,y,z)k defined on C, we have

∫CF⋅dr=∫CP(x,y,z)dx+Q(x,y,z)dy+R(x,y,z)dz.

Therefore, in our case, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫Cyzdx+xzdy+xydz.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}x+{e}^{x}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Let $F(x,y)={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ and let $C$ be the path defined by $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t-1⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$
question.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}x+{e}^{x}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Let F(x,y)=eyi+exj and let C be the path defined by r(t)=⟨t2,t−1⟩ for t∈[0,1]. Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr?

a
∫Ceydx+exdy
b
∫Cey2dx+ex−1dy
c
∫Cex−1dx+ey2dy
d
∫Cex+ydxdy
e
∫Cex2dx+ey−1dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a piecewise-smooth path C and a vector field F(x,y)=P(x,y)i+Q(x,y)j

defined on C, we have ∫CF⋅dr=∫CP(x,y)dx+Q(x,y)dy.

Therefore, in our case, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫Ceydx+exdy.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Establishing the Connection With Line Integrals of Scalar Fields
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}4\,\text{d}x-(2y-3x)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Let F(x,y)=4i−(2y−3x)j and let C be the path defined by r(t)=⟨t,3t−1⟩ for t∈[0,1]. Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr?

a
∫C(3x−1)dx+ydy
b
∫Cxdx+(3y−1)dy
c
∫C4dx−(2y−3x)dy
d
∫C(3y−1)dx+xdy
e
 ∫C(2y−3x)dx−4dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a piecewise-smooth path C and a vector field F(x,y)=P(x,y)i+Q(x,y)j

defined on C, we have ∫CF⋅dr=∫CP(x,y)dx+Q(x,y)dy.

Therefore, in our case, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫C4dx−(2y−3x)dy.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}(x-3y)\,\text{d}x+2\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorial.name: Reversing the Orientation of a Curve and Sums Over Unions of Paths
tutorial.problem:
Since there is a fundamental link between line integrals of vector-valued functions and line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y,$ it should be unsurprising that they share similar properties. We list two of them below:

- If $-C$ denotes the path obtained by reversing the orientation of $C,$ then

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

- If $C = C_1\cup C_2$ is the union of two paths $C_1$ and $C_2$, then

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r 
= 
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

The first property has an intuitive meaning if we think about it in terms of the work done by a force on a particle. To see this, consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the line segment $\overline{AB},$ shown below. Let $C$ be the path defined by traversing the line segment from $A$ to $B.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/4f69f80d98d301410908f7ec867a89bdc834c22a51f224d9b00b80ceca39ab87.png)

 

Let $W(C)$ be the work done in moving the particle along $C.$ Since our particle moves in the same direction as the vector field, we have

$$
W(C) = \int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r > 0.
$$

However, if we move the particle from $B$ to $A,$ we expect the line integral to be negative. This is because the particle is now moving against $\mathbf F.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/fe6b2e67d33a4993104406c88b1dc0dc897be33d034007ed581a75f741ddf620.png)

 

Therefore,

$$
W(-C) = \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r < 0.
$$

We can show that the work done in moving the particle along $-C$ is the same as the work done in moving it along $C$ but with the opposite sign. That is

$$
W(-C) = -W(C).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$
tutorial.content:
Since there is a fundamental link between line integrals of vector-valued functions and line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y,$ it should be unsurprising that they share similar properties. We list two of them below:

- If $-C$ denotes the path obtained by reversing the orientation of $C,$ then

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

- If $C = C_1\cup C_2$ is the union of two paths $C_1$ and $C_2$, then

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r 
= 
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

The first property has an intuitive meaning if we think about it in terms of the work done by a force on a particle. To see this, consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the line segment $\overline{AB},$ shown below. Let $C$ be the path defined by traversing the line segment from $A$ to $B.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/4f69f80d98d301410908f7ec867a89bdc834c22a51f224d9b00b80ceca39ab87.png)

 

Let $W(C)$ be the work done in moving the particle along $C.$ Since our particle moves in the same direction as the vector field, we have

$$
W(C) = \int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r > 0.
$$

However, if we move the particle from $B$ to $A,$ we expect the line integral to be negative. This is because the particle is now moving against $\mathbf F.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/fe6b2e67d33a4993104406c88b1dc0dc897be33d034007ed581a75f741ddf620.png)

 

Therefore,

$$
W(-C) = \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r < 0.
$$

We can show that the work done in moving the particle along $-C$ is the same as the work done in moving it along $C$ but with the opposite sign. That is

$$
W(-C) = -W(C).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

Question 6
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path OABO, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?

a
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
b
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
c
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
d
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
e
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can represent C, which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of 3 paths:

C=C1∪{−C2}∪C3,

where −C2 is the same path as C2 but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr+∫−C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup \{-{C}_{2}\}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ is the same path as ${C}_{2}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path LMNL, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?

a
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
b
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
c
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
d
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
e
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can represent C, which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of 3 paths:

C=C1∪{−C2}∪C3,

where −C2 is the same path as C2 but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr+∫−C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr.

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C=\{-{C}_{1}\}\cup {C}_{2}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{1}$ is the same path as ${C}_{1}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path PQRP, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?

a
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
b
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
c
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
d
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
e
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can represent C, which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of 3 paths:

C={−C1}∪C2∪C3,

where −C1 is the same path as C1 but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫−C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr=−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr.

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C=\{-{C}_{1}\}\cup {C}_{2}\cup \{-{C}_{3}\},
$$

where $-{C}_{1}$ and $-{C}_{3}$ are the same paths as ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{3}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path ABCA, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the clockwise direction?

a
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
b
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
c
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
d
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
e
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can represent C, which is traversed clockwise, as the union of 3 paths:

C={−C1}∪C2∪{−C3},

where −C1 and −C3 are the same paths as C1 and C3 but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫−C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫−C3F⋅dr=−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C=\{-{C}_{1}\}\cup {C}_{2}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{1}$ is the same path as ${C}_{1}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path TUVT, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the clockwise direction?

a
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
b
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
c
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
d
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
e
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can represent C, which is traversed in clockwise, as the union of 3 paths:

C={−C1}∪C2∪C3,

where −C1 is the same path as C1 but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫−C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr=−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr.
